Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Orthogonal and Unitary Groups) Let $F$ be a local field of characteristic 0. Define the classical groups $G = \mathrm{SO}(V)$ for a quadratic space $V$ over $F$, and $G = \mathrm{U}(V)$ for a Hermitian space $V$ over a quadratic extension $E/F$.
Hint
Quadratic forms are symmetric bilinear pairings; Hermitian forms satisfy $\langle x, y \rangle = \tau(\langle y, x \rangle)$ for the non-trivial automorphism $\tau \in \operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Subgroups and Codimension 1 Pairs) Let $W \subset V$ be a non-degenerate subspace of codimension 1. Define the subgroup embedding $H \subset G$, where $H = \mathrm{SO}(W)$ into $G = \mathrm{SO}(V)$, or $H = \mathrm{U}(W)$ into $G = \mathrm{U}(V)$.
Hint
$H$ is the stabilizer in $G$ of a non-zero orthogonal vector $v_0 \in W^\perp$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Bessel and Fourier-Jacobi Models) Distinguish the two geometric settings of the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjectures: the Bessel case (codimension 1 embeddings $H \hookrightarrow G$) and the Fourier–Jacobi case (symplectic and metaplectic groups $\mathrm{Sp}(W) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Sp}(V)$).
Hint
The Bessel case concerns spherical pairs with trivial unipotent radicals, while Fourier–Jacobi pairs involve Heisenberg unipotent radicals
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(The Hom Space of Intertwiners) Let $\pi$ be an irreducible admissible representation of $G(F)$ and $\sigma$ an irreducible admissible representation of $H(F)$. Define the branching space $\operatorname{Hom}_{H(F)}(\pi \otimes \sigma, \mathbb{C})$.
Hint
Elements are continuous linear functionals $\ell: \pi \otimes \sigma \to \mathbb{C}$ satisfying $\ell(\pi(h)v \otimes \sigma(h)w) = \ell(v \otimes w)$ for all $h \in H(F)$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Multiplicity One Theorems) State the local multiplicity one theorem (proved by Aizenbud–Gourevitch–Rallis–Schiffmann and Waldspurger) for orthogonal and unitary groups: $\dim \operatorname{Hom}_{H(F)}(\pi \otimes \sigma, \mathbb{C}) \le 1$.
Hint
The pair $(G \times H, \operatorname{diag}(H))$ is a Gelfand pair, meaning the invariant distribution space on the double coset is 1-dimensional
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(The Local Langlands Correspondence) Let $W_F'$ be the Weil–Deligne group of $F$. State the Local Langlands Correspondence mapping an irreducible admissible representation $\pi$ of $G(F)$ to an $L$-parameter $\phi: W_F' \to {}^L G$.
Hint
${}^L G = G^\vee(\mathbb{C}) \rtimes W_F$ is the Langlands dual group, where $\mathrm{SO}(2n+1)^\vee \cong \operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(\mathbb{C})$ and $\mathrm{SO}(2n)^\vee \cong \mathrm{SO}_{2n}(\mathbb{C})$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Local L-Packets) Define a local $L$-packet $\Pi_\phi(G)$ as the finite set of irreducible representations of $G(F)$ sharing the same $L$-parameter $\phi$.
Hint
For quasi-split groups, $L$-packets are partitioned into distinct representations parameterized by the characters of the component group of the centralizer of $\phi$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(The Component Group S_\phi) Let $\phi: W_F' \to {}^L G$ be an $L$-parameter. Define the centralizer group $C_\phi = \operatorname{Cent}( \operatorname{im}(\phi), G^\vee )$ and its finite component group $S_\phi = C_\phi / C_\phi^\circ Z(G^\vee)$.
Hint
For orthogonal and unitary groups, $S_\phi$ is an elementary abelian 2-group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^k$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Vogan Packets and Pure Inner Forms) Explain why the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjectures require working with Vogan packets across all pure inner forms of $G$ and $H$.
Hint
A Vogan packet is the disjoint union $\Pi_\phi = \bigsqcup_{G'} \Pi_\phi(G')$ over all pure inner forms $G'$ of $G$; working with Vogan packets guarantees that the branching space is non-zero for a unique pair in the packet
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Character Parameterization of Representations in a Packet) For a generic $L$-packet $\Pi_\phi$, state the bijection $\Pi_\phi \longleftrightarrow \widehat{S}_\phi$ between representations $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$ and irreducible characters $\eta \in \widehat{S}_\phi = \operatorname{Hom}(S_\phi, \{\pm 1\})$.
Hint
The trivial character corresponds to the unique generic/unramified representation in the packet associated with a fixed Whittaker datum
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(The Local GGP Conjecture Formulation) Let $\phi$ and $\psi$ be generic $L$-parameters for $G$ and $H$, respectively. State the local Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture: $$\sum_{\pi \in \Pi_\phi, \, \sigma \in \Pi_\psi} \dim \operatorname{Hom}_{H(F)}(\pi \otimes \sigma, \mathbb{C}) = 1.$$
Hint
There is a unique representation $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$ and a unique representation $\sigma \in \Pi_\psi$ on a unique pair of inner forms $(G', H')$ such that $\operatorname{Hom}_{H'(F)}(\pi \otimes \sigma, \mathbb{C})$ is exactly 1-dimensional
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Distinguished Characters and Local Root Numbers) How is the unique pair $(\pi, \sigma)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_H(\pi \otimes \sigma, \mathbb{C}) \ne 0$ characterized via characters of $S_\phi \times S_\psi$?
Hint
The pair is selected by a specific character $\eta = (\epsilon_1, \dots, \epsilon_k) \in \widehat{S}_\phi \times \widehat{S}_\psi$ computed explicitly from local Deligne–Langlands epsilon factors $\epsilon(1/2, \phi_i \otimes \psi_j, \psi_F)$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Rankin-Selberg L-Functions for Product Parameters) Let $\phi: W_F' \to \mathrm{GL}(M)$ and $\psi: W_F' \to \mathrm{GL}(N)$ be the standard representations of the $L$-parameters. Define the Rankin–Selberg tensor product $L$-function $L(s, \phi \otimes \psi)$ and its local root number $\epsilon(s, \phi \otimes \psi, \psi_F)$.
Hint
The local root number at the central critical point $s = 1/2$ takes values in $\{\pm 1\}$ and dictates the local branching law
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(The Global GGP Conjecture: Period Integrals) Let $F$ be a global number field with adèle ring $\mathbb{A}_F$. For automorphic cusp forms $\varphi \in \pi$ on $G(\mathbb{A}_F)$ and $\phi \in \sigma$ on $H(\mathbb{A}_F)$, define the global period integral: $$\mathcal{P}(\varphi, \phi) = \int_{H(F) \backslash H(\mathbb{A}_F)} \varphi(h) \phi(h) \, dh.$$
Hint
The non-vanishing of $\mathcal{P}(\varphi, \phi)$ measures the non-triviality of the global branching law $\pi|_{H(\mathbb{A}_F)}$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(The Central L-Value Formula: Global GGP) State the global Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture relating the period integral $\mathcal{P}(\varphi, \phi)$ to the central value of the automorphic tensor product $L$-function: $$\frac{|\mathcal{P}(\varphi, \phi)|^2}{\langle \varphi, \varphi \rangle \langle \phi, \phi \rangle} = C \cdot \frac{L(1/2, \pi \otimes \sigma)}{L(1, \pi, \operatorname{Ad}) L(1, \sigma, \operatorname{Ad})}.$$
Hint
The global period is non-zero on the cuspidal packet if and only if $L(1/2, \pi \otimes \sigma) \ne 0$ and the local conditions are satisfied at all places $v$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Waldspurger's Theorem as GGP for SO(3) x SO(2)) Show that when $G = \mathrm{SO}(3) \cong \mathrm{PGL}_2$ and $H = \mathrm{SO}(2)$ (a torus $T$ associated with a quadratic extension), the GGP conjecture reduces to Waldspurger's classical formula for toric periods and central $L$-values $L(1/2, \pi \otimes \chi)$.

The local packet of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ consists of representations of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(F)$ and its inner form $D^\times / F^\times$ for a quaternion division algebra $D$
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Gross-Zagier Formula as the Arithmetic GGP) Explain how the arithmetic Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture generalizes the Gross–Zagier theorem on heights of Heegner points: when $L(1/2, \pi \otimes \sigma) = 0$, the first derivative $L'(1/2, \pi \otimes \sigma)$ is proportional to the Néron–Tate height of an arithmetic cycle on a Shimura variety.

The classical period integral is replaced by the arithmetic intersection pairing of special cycles on unitary/orthogonal Shimura varieties
https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Theta Correspondence and Local Packets) Explain the role of the local Howe correspondence (theta lift) between dual reductive pairs $(G, G')$ in constructing representations inside local GGP packets.
Hint

https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/ggp9.pdf
Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross
(Epsilon Factor Parity and Obstructions) Prove that the global root number $\epsilon(1/2, \pi \otimes \sigma) = \prod_v \epsilon_v(1/2, \pi_v \otimes \sigma_v, \psi_v)$ must equal $+1$ for the global period integral to be non-zero on the quasi-split form.

Sur les Conjectures de Gross-Prasad by Benedict Gross

State and justify: "homeomorphisms are affine."
Hint

State and justify: "morphisms with affine source and target are affine."
Hint
if X is affine, then for every affine open V ⊂ Y, f^{-1}(V) ⊂ X is a subscheme of an affine scheme; but more simply, when X itself is affine, f^{-1}(V) is affine automatically because f factors through Spec of the coordinate ring and a closed/open condition is not even needed — the whole preimage X is affine so any subscheme argument is unnecessary; formally: the composite Spec(A) → X → Y with X affine makes f automatically affine since affineness of the source scheme is inherited by all preimages via base change to affine opens of an affine scheme.

It is finite (hence affine, proper, projective by "finite morphisms are projective") and quasi-finite, but it is ramified at the origin in characteristic $\ne 2$ (the fiber over 0 is a single point with multiplicity 2, i.e. $\Omega^1\ne0$ there), so it fails "definition étale" and fails "universally injective morphisms are injective" in the converse direction (it is injective in char 2 in a purely-inseparable sense but not universally injective in char $\ne 2$ since a base change to $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ still identifies $\pm\sqrt{a}$ as two distinct preimages for $a\ne0$) — a clean example separating "finite" and "quasi-finite" from "étale" and "universally injective."

Is "twisted square from $\mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q}$ to $\mathbb{P}^1_\mathbb{Q}$" proper? Is it a closed immersion?
Hint
The target $\mathbb{P}^1_\mathbb{Q}$ is proper over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}$, but the morphism from the (non-proper) affine line into it cannot itself be proper unless its image is closed and the map is universally closed onto that image with proper fibers; since $\mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q}$ is not proper over $\mathbb{Q}$, and the composite $\mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{P}^1_\mathbb{Q}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}$ is not proper (else $\mathbb{A}^1$ would be proper by "universally closed morphisms are closed" composed appropriately), the twisted square map itself is not proper; it also is not a closed immersion since $\mathbb{A}^1_\mathbb{Q}$ is not compact/closed in $\mathbb{P}^1_\mathbb{Q}$ under the usual affine chart embedding twisted by the given data.

Is "degenerating family of conics" flat? Is every fiber regular?
Hint
Such a family (e.g. $xy = t$ degenerating to $xy=0$ at $t=0$) is typically flat over the parameter line (flatness for hypersurfaces of constant degree is automatic, by the standard criterion that a family of hypersurfaces of fixed degree in a fixed ambient projective/affine space is flat), yet the fiber at $t=0$ (the union of two lines, a node) is singular, so "regular morphisms are flat" cannot be reversed: flat does not imply regular fibers, only the other direction (built into the definition) holds.

Is "finite fibers" equivalent to "quasi-finite"? Use the database's definitions to pin down the discrepancy
Hint
They differ by finiteness conditions on the morphism itself. "Injective morphisms have finite fibers" shows finite fibers is a weak, purely set-theoretic condition following from injectivity alone. "Definition quasi-finite" additionally requires the morphism to be of finite type (or finite presentation) with locally finite fibers, a scheme-theoretic condition. An example distinguishing them: $\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}$ has finite (indeed infinite but each residue field finite over the base only in the algebraic sense) — more precisely $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}(x) \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}$ has one point with infinite residue field extension, so it has "finite fibers" as a set but is not quasi-finite since it fails finite type.

The step "finite is proper and affine" is redundant once you have "finite is proper and quasi-finite," since either one alone recovers properness; either theorem may be skipped.

The database lists $\operatorname{Spec}\left(\prod_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Q}\right)$ as an example scheme. Determine whether it is Noetherian, and use "Hilbert basis theorem" and "definition Noetherian" to justify your answer, then explain why $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^\infty \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q} \to \operatorname{Spec}\left(\prod_{i=1}^\infty\mathbb{Q}\right)$ is relevant
Hint
$\prod_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Q}$ is not Noetherian: the chain of ideals $I_n = \{(a_i) : a_i = 0 \text{ for } i \le n\}$ is strictly increasing and never stabilizes, violating the ascending chain condition in "definition Noetherian." The Hilbert basis theorem only guarantees Noetherianity is preserved under finitely generated polynomial extensions of Noetherian rings, which does not apply to this infinite product. The disjoint union map is the natural comparison map from the "constructible" countable disjoint union into the Zariski spectrum of the product ring, illustrating that $\operatorname{Spec}$ of an infinite product has "extra" points (ultrafilter points) beyond the union of the factors.

Neither. Since they are not immersions at all, "surjective immersions are closed immersions" does not apply — the surjectivity alone is insufficient without the immersion hypothesis.

Hint
No. The quotient map is ramified exactly along the diagonal $\{x=y\}$, where the stabilizer is nontrivial ($\mathbb{Z}/2$), so the residue field extension / tangent map fails the infinitesimal lifting criterion for formal étaleness there, i.e. $\Omega^1_{X/Y} \ne 0$ along the diagonal. It is locally of finite presentation (finite morphism of finite type schemes) but fails formal étaleness, hence by "étale is formally étale and locally of finite presentation" it cannot be étale, even though it is étale away from the diagonal.

The scheme $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,\ldots]/(x_i^2 - x_i,\, x_ix_j : i\ne j)$ is listed in the database. Is it Noetherian? Is it reduced? Use these to test "excellent schemes are locally Noetherian" vacuously or not
Hint
It is reduced, since the relations $x_i^2=x_i$ and $x_ix_j=0$ generate a radical ideal (a Boolean-type ring, isomorphic to functions on a countable discrete set with a basepoint). It is NOT Noetherian, since the ideal $(x_1,x_2,\ldots)$ is not finitely generated (infinitely many independent idempotent-like generators). Consequently it cannot be excellent, since "excellent schemes are locally Noetherian" forces excellence to fail here — this scheme is a genuine witness that reduced does not imply Noetherian, hence not excellent.

Hint
A finite locally free morphism is simultaneously proper (hence universally closed) AND universally open (from flat + locally of finite presentation), so its image in each connected component is a union of connected components — i.e. finite locally free morphisms are "clopen" onto unions of components of the target. This is consistent with "finite morphisms with affine target are H-projective," since H-projective morphisms are always proper, and here properness is independently confirmed via the finite $\Rightarrow$ proper route.

No — $\mathbb{Q}[x^q : q\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}]$ is generated by infinitely many independent monomials with fractional exponents, so as a $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra it is not finitely generated, hence $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}[x^q:q\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}] \to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}$ fails "definition of finite type" (finite type requires a surjection from a polynomial ring in finitely many variables). Segal's Gamma rings
Compute the extension of the field with one element $\mathbb{F}_1$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ via Borger's $\Lambda$-rings
https://alainconnes.org/wp-content/uploads/segals-GammaRings.pdf
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(1) To organise Galois groups and modules, how does one formulate a classical class formation?
Hint
A class formation is a pair $(\Gamma, A)$ where $\Gamma$ is a profinite group and $A$ is a discrete $\Gamma$-module such that for every open subgroup $H \subset \Gamma$ and open normal subgroup $N \triangleleft H$, $H^1(H/N, A^N) = 0$ and $H^2(H/N, A^N) \cong \frac{1}{[H:N]}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$ canonically via an invariant map $\mathrm{inv}_{H/N}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(2) How does one establish the vanishing of $H^1(H/N, A^N)$ and the cyclicity of $H^2(H/N, A^N)$?
Hint
By studying the Galois fixed-point modules $A^N$ across finite Galois extensions and computing the Herbrand quotient $h(A^N) = [H:N]$ for cyclic steps using Hilbert's Theorem 90 for the $H^1$-vanishing.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(3) What is the purpose of the Nakayama-Tate lemma in class formations?
Hint
Given a class formation with fundamental class $\alpha \in H^2(G, A)$, cup product with $\alpha$ yields an isomorphism $\widehat{H}^i(G, \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \widehat{H}^{i+2}(G, A)$ for all $i \in \mathbb{Z}$; taking $i = -2$ gives the Artin reciprocity isomorphism $(G)^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong \widehat{H}^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \widehat{H}^0(G, A) = A^G / \mathrm{Tr}_G(A)$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(4) How does one verify that a given Galois module satisfies the Nakayama-Tate condition?
Hint
Check that for every Sylow $p$-subgroup $G_p \subset G$, $H^1(G_p, A) = 0$ and $H^2(G_p, A)$ is cyclic of order $|G_p|$, generated by the restriction of the fundamental class $\alpha$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(5) How does one construct the Artin reciprocity map with dense image and determine its kernel?
Hint
Taking the projective limit over all open normal subgroups $N \triangleleft H$ of the Nakayama-Tate isomorphisms $(H/N)^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong A^H / \mathrm{Tr}_{H/N}(A^N)$ yields the Artin map $A^H \to H^{\mathrm{ab}}$ with dense image and kernel $\bigcap_{N} \mathrm{Tr}_{H/N}(A^N)$, which is the subgroup of universal norms.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(6) What is the image of the global/local Artin map $A^H \to H^{\mathrm{ab}}$?
Hint
The image is dense in $H^{\mathrm{ab}}$, and the map induces a topological isomorphism $\widehat{A^H} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{\mathrm{ab}}$ on the appropriate completion (the profinite completion for local fields / idèle class groups).
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(7) What are the axiomatic cohomological criteria required for a class formation?
Hint
(i) $H^1(H/N, A^N) = 0$; (ii) there exists an isomorphism $\mathrm{inv}_{H/N} \colon H^2(H/N, A^N) \xrightarrow{\sim} \frac{1}{[H:N]}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$; (iii) these invariant maps commute with inflation and restriction maps across all open subgroups $N \subset H \subset \Gamma$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(8) How does one reduce the verification of class formation axioms to cyclic extensions?
Hint
By Sylow theory and solvable filtration, any finite group can be decomposed into a tower of cyclic extensions of prime degree; checking the axioms on prime-degree cyclic steps implies them for all finite Galois extensions.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(9) How is Tate cohomology exploited via 2-periodicity for cyclic groups?
Hint
For cyclic $G$, $\widehat{H}^{i}(G, A) \cong \widehat{H}^{i+2}(G, A)$ for all $i$, so the entire cohomology is determined by $\widehat{H}^0(G, A) = A^G / \mathrm{Nm}(A)$ and $\widehat{H}^1(G, A) = \ker(\mathrm{Nm}) / I_G A$, simplifying all calculations to the Herbrand quotient $h(A) = |\widehat{H}^0(A)| / |\widehat{H}^1(A)|$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(10) What ingredients are required to show a module forms a class formation?
Hint
One needs: (1) vanishing of $H^1$ via Hilbert's Theorem 90 / Kummer theory; (2) computation of Herbrand quotients $h(A^N) = [H:N]$; (3) existence of enough cyclic extensions (especially unramified ones) to normalize and assemble the invariant maps.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(11) How is local class field theory proved using class formations for nonarchimedean local fields?
Hint
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the Galois category of finite separable extensions of $K$, with coefficient functor $A(L) = L^\times$. (1) $H^1(L/K, L^\times) = 0$ by Hilbert 90; (2) for unramified extensions, $h(\mathcal{O}_L^\times) = 1$ implies $h(L^\times) = [L:K]$; (3) unramified invariant maps extend to all extensions, proving local CFT.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(12) Why is the classical definition of class formations non-canonical, and how does the basepoint problem arise?
Hint
The absolute Galois group $\Gamma$ requires choosing an algebraic closure $\overline{k}$, making $\Gamma$ defined only up to non-unique inner automorphism; the Galois category is an étale/connected groupoid, not an intrinsically based group.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(13) How does one generate enough cyclic extensions to establish class formations when roots of unity are missing?
Hint
Adjoin roots of unity and apply Kummer theory, using the non-degeneracy of the Kummer pairing $K^\times / (K^\times)^n \times \mathrm{Gal}(K(\sqrt[n]{K})/K) \to \mu_n$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(14) What is the Weil group of a class formation and how does it resolve the canonicity issue?
Hint
The Weil group $W_{L/K}$ is the group extension $1 \to A^L \to W_{L/K} \to \mathrm{Gal}(L/K) \to 1$ classified by the fundamental class $\alpha \in H^2(\mathrm{Gal}(L/K), A^L)$; Clausen refines this into an abelian gerbe on $B\Gamma$ banded by $A$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(15) How are cocycle classes and 2-morphisms interpreted at the chain level for gerbes?
Hint
A 2-cocycle is $x \in C^2$ with $dx = 0$ representing the extension class; a 1-cochain $\alpha \in C^1$ with $d\alpha = y - x$ defines a 1-isomorphism (2-morphism of extensions) between cocycles $x$ and $y$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(16) How are isomorphism classes of gerbes defined using 2-groupoids?
Hint
The 2-category of groupoids forms a $(2, 1)$-category where gerbes banded by $A$ over a site $\mathcal{C}$ are classified by $\pi_0 \mathrm{Map}(\mathcal{C}, B^2 A) \cong H^2(\mathcal{C}, A)$, with 1-morphisms being $A$-torsor equivalences and 2-morphisms being $A$-translations.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(17) What are the objects, 1-morphisms, and 2-morphisms in the categorical presentation of the Weil group?
Hint
Objects are inverse systems of group extensions $1 \to A^N \to E_N \to H/N \to 1$; 1-morphisms are morphisms of inverse systems compatible with projection to $H/N$; 2-morphisms are conjugations by elements of the abelian kernel $A^N$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(18) What is a refined class formation in the sense of Clausen/Scholze?
Hint
A triple $(\mathcal{C}, F, \alpha)$ where $\mathcal{C}$ is a Galois category, $F \colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z})$ is a cosheaf valued in the derived $\infty$-category of condensed/discrete abelian groups such that $H_i(F(X)) = 0$ for $i \neq 0, 1$, and $\alpha \colon H_0(F(X)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{Z}$ is an isomorphism for every connected object $X \in \mathcal{C}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(19) How does one promote a classical class formation to a refined class formation?
Hint
Construct a map $\kappa \colon \mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{R}\Gamma(\mathcal{C}, A)[2]$ in $\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z})$—where $\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C} = \bigcup_{X} \frac{1}{|X|}\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q}$—such that $\kappa$ induces an isomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C})/\mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{\sim} H^2(\mathcal{C}, A)$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(20) What are the homotopy groups $\pi_0, \pi_1, \pi_2$ of the mapping space classifying promotions to refined class formations?
Hint
$\pi_0$ is the set of compatible fundamental classes in $\mathrm{Hom}((\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C})/\mathbb{Z}, H^2(\mathcal{C}, A))$; $\pi_1$ is the torsor under $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C}, A(*))$; $\pi_2$ is $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C}, A(*))$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(21) Why must $F$ be defined as a cosheaf, and how does this relate to its transpose $F^{\mathrm{tr}}$?
Hint
The homology invariant $H_1(F(X)) = A(X)$ assigns to a Galois cover its units/class group via pushforwards/norms, so $F$ is covariant on $\mathcal{C}$ (a cosheaf); its linear dual/transpose $F^{\mathrm{tr}} = \mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(F, \mathbb{Z})$ is a contravariant sheaf on $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(22) How does the refined class formation work for the base field $\mathbb{Q}$?
Hint
$H^2(G_\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}^\times / \mathbb{Q}^\times) \cong \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ has two choices of sign (homology/geometric Frobenius vs. cohomology/arithmetic Frobenius); $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}^\times / \mathbb{Q}^\times) = 0$, and $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}^\times / \mathbb{Q}^\times) \cong \mathbb{R}_{>0}^\times$, which contracts upon passing to norm-1 idèles, giving a canonical refined class formation.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(23) How does one obtain canonical refined class formations for general number fields from $\mathbb{Q}$?
Hint
By restricting the canonical refined class formation of $\mathbb{Q}$ along the finite étale slice $\mathcal{C}_K \subset \mathcal{C}_\mathbb{Q}$; the lift is unique up to an isomorphism that is unique up to powers of Frobenius.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(24) How are refined class formations constructed for finite fields and nonarchimedean local fields?
Hint
For $k = \mathbb{F}_q$ or a nonarchimedean local field $K$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/\#\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O}_K^\times) \cong \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}/\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathrm{Hom} = 0$; fixing the canonical Frobenius generator gives a canonical lift to a refined class formation.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(25) How does one handle archimedean local fields $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ in refined class formations?
Hint
For $\mathbb{R}$, the Galois group is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$; $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{R}^\times) = 0$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{R}^\times) \cong \mathbb{R}^\times / \{\pm 1\} \cong \mathbb{R}_{>0}^\times$, which is canonically trivialized by taking positive norms.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(26) How do operations on refined class formations behave under base change?
Hint
Under a morphism of sites/Galois categories $f \colon \mathcal{C}' \to \mathcal{C}$, the pullback of a refined class formation is obtained by derived pushforward of the cosheaf $f_* F$, preserving the axioms.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(27) How does one define class field theory universally for locally compact Hausdorff number rings $R$?
Hint
Define an $\infty$-functor $F^{\mathrm{univ}}$ on the finite étale site of $R$ with $H_0(F^{\mathrm{univ}}(R)) = \mathbb{Z}$ and $H_1(F^{\mathrm{univ}}(R)) = C(R)$, the topological class group of $R$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(28) What are the classical class groups recovered by $H_1(F^{\mathrm{univ}}(R))$ across different rings $R$?
Hint
(1) Local field: $K^\times$; (2) Local ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$: $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$; (3) Finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$: $\mathbb{Z}$; (4) Global ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$: $\mathrm{Pic}(\mathcal{O}_K)$; (5) Global field $K$: idèle class group $C_K = \mathbb{A}_K^\times / K^\times$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(29) How does $K$-theory of locally compact modules universally produce class field theory?
Hint
The condensed $K$-theory spectrum $K(\mathbf{LCA}_R)$ of locally compact $R$-modules satisfies $K_1(\mathbf{LCA}_R) \cong C(R)$ (the class group), while $K_0(\mathbf{LCA}_R)$ contains topological dimension data that can be normalized to $\mathbb{Z}$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Weil-Moore Anima (lecture 2)
(30) How does the refined class formation assemble into the global Weil groupoid $\mathcal{W}$?
Hint
The gerbes over finite Galois quotients form an inverse system of topological 2-groupoids indexed by finite étale covers; taking the 2-limit $\mathcal{W} = \varprojlim_N E_N$ yields the Weil groupoid, whose connectedness ($\pi_0 \mathcal{W} = *$) follows from the compactness of the idèle class groups.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11950
Goncharov
(Free Algebra Commutator) Let $V = \mathbb{C} x \oplus \mathbb{C} y$. In the tensor algebra $T(V)$, write down the commutator $[x, y]$.

By definition, $[a, b] = a \otimes b - b \otimes a$
https://arxiv.org/pdf/0803.0297
Goncharov

Hint
The difference $x \otimes y - y \otimes x = [x, y]$ lies in the commutator subspace, so its class in the quotient is zero
https://arxiv.org/pdf/0803.0297
Goncharov

Hint
In an associative algebra there are $3! = 6$ words. Modulo cyclic shifts $(x_0 x_1 x_2 \sim x_1 x_2 x_0 \sim x_2 x_0 x_1)$, there are $(3-1)! = 2$ independent cyclic words: $C(x_0 \otimes x_1 \otimes x_2)$ and $C(x_0 \otimes x_2 \otimes x_1)$
https://arxiv.org/pdf/0803.0297
Goncharov
(The Shuffle Product) Compute the shuffle product of the two single-letter words $(x_1) \ Sha (x_2)$.

https://arxiv.org/pdf/0803.0297

Hint
Fix the first element $x_0$ and shuffle the remaining set $\{x_1\}$ with $\{x_2\}$: $C(x_0 \otimes (x_1 \ Sha x_2)) = C(x_0 \otimes x_1 \otimes x_2) + C(x_0 \otimes x_2 \otimes x_1) = 0$

Goncharov

https://arxiv.org/pdf/0803.0297
Goncharov
(Dimension Count for Lie Words) Using the shuffle relation $C(x_0 \otimes x_1 \otimes x_2) + C(x_0 \otimes x_2 \otimes x_1) = 0$, prove that the space of cyclic Lie words of length 3 on three distinct letters is 1-dimensional.

foundations of categorical measures
Why does uncountable measure theory adopt a Baire-centric rather than Borel-centric philosophy?
Hint
In non-metrizable spaces, the Borel $\sigma$-algebra is too large and points/compact sets may fail to be $G_\delta$ and we do consider this when say one does integration theory or when considering the Baire category theorem where the intersection of countably many dense sets is a dense countable intersection of open sets; the Baire $\sigma$-algebras $C_0\text{-}\mathrm{Baire}(X)$ and $C_b\text{-}\mathrm{Baire}(X)$ are generated by continuous functions and interact naturally with functional analysis. One needs a theorem for compact spaces to extend Baire measures to unique regular Borel measures. Baire sigma algebras as a property is preserved under product and will remain restricted to countably determined sets and will not have nonmeasurable topologies. See page 7 for all the tradeoffs.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00681
foundations of categorical measures
How is a Radon probability measure defined via inner regularity on an LCH space?
Hint
A probability measure $\mu$ on $C_0\text{-}\mathrm{Baire}(X)$ or $\mathrm{Borel}(X)$ is Radon if it is inner regular with respect to compact $G_\delta$ sets, meaning $\mu(E) = \sup \{ \mu(K) : K \subset E, K \text{ compact } G_\delta \}$. We need this definition of Radon measures to characterise the regularity properties of the measure we get from Riesz duality of locally compact Hausdorff spaces

Hint
The Riesz representation theorem allows one to start with a positive linear functional in the space of continuous compactly supported functions on $X$ and a locally compact Hausdorff space and guarantees that there is a Radon measure at least on it. The Radon measure is the probability measure for locally compact Hausdorff spaces.

How did Emmy Noether conceptualize Betti numbers in the development of homology?
Hint
Noether showed that Betti numbers are numeric shadows of the underlying homology groups $H_n(X)$, which are abelian groups measuring the difference between closed cycles and exact boundaries; homology is a strictly richer algebraic invariant that cannot be recovered from Betti numbers alone.

Hint
The zeta function $\zeta_X(T) = \exp\left(\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})}{n} T^n\right)$ packages point counts over all finite extensions; Weil's proof for curves and his conjectures for higher-dimensional varieties predicted that $\zeta_X(T)$ is a rational function whose zeroes and poles are governed by a well-behaved Weil cohomology theory ($\ell$-adic étale cohomology).

Hint
Let $p \colon X \to *$ be the structure map. (1) Cohomology: $C^*(X) = p_* p^*(\mathbf{1})$; (2) Compactly supported cohomology: $C_c^*(X) = p_! p^*(\mathbf{1})$; (3) Borel-Moore homology: $C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X) = p_* p^!(\mathbf{1})$; (4) Homology with compact supports: $C_*(X) = p_! p^!(\mathbf{1})$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How does Verdier duality operate between these four theories via the dualizing object $\omega_X = p^!\mathbf{1}$?
Hint
The adjunctions induce a canonical pairing $\mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(p_! p^* \mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}) \simeq p_* \mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(p^* \mathbf{1}, p^! \mathbf{1}) = p_* p^! \mathbf{1}$, identifying the dual of compactly supported cohomology $C_c^*(X)^\vee$ with Borel-Moore homology $C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(X)$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How do different geometric coefficient systems determine specific cohomology theories?
Hint
(1) Constructible $\ell$-adic sheaves $\mathcal{D}_c^b(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell) \implies$ étale cohomology; (2) Constructible topological sheaves $\mathcal{D}_c^b(X^{\mathrm{an}}, \Lambda) \implies$ Betti cohomology; (3) Holonomic $\mathcal{D}$-modules $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{hol}}^b(\mathcal{D}_X) \implies$ algebraic de Rham cohomology; (4) Voevodsky motives $\mathcal{DM}(X) \implies$ motivic cohomology.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How are vanishing/nearby cycle functors, Chern classes, and regulator maps viewed in the six-functor context?
Hint
Nearby/vanishing cycles are specialized gluing functors across degenerations; Chern classes and cycle/regulator maps are natural transformations between different six-functor coefficient systems (e.g., from motivic cohomology to étale or de Rham cohomology).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What does proper pushforward mean for the transformation $f_! \to f_*$?
Hint
The canonical "forget supports" natural transformation $\alpha_f \colon f_! \to f_*$ is an isomorphism if and only if $f$ is proper.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How does Grothendieck duality specialize to Poincaré and Serre dualities?
Hint
For a smooth morphism $f \colon X \to *$, relative purity computes $f^!\mathbf{1} \simeq \mathbf{1}(d)[2d]$; for $\ell$-adic coefficients, this yields $H^n(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell)^\vee \cong H_c^{2d-n}(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell(d))$ (Poincaré duality), and for coherent sheaves on proper $X$, it yields $\mathrm{Ext}^i(\mathcal{F}, \omega_X) \cong H^{n-i}(X, \mathcal{F})^\vee$ (Serre duality).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is the proper projection formula and what does it assert?
Hint
For any morphism $f \colon X \to Y$, there is a natural isomorphism $f_!(A \otimes^{\mathbf{L}} f^*B) \xrightarrow{\sim} f_!(A) \otimes^{\mathbf{L}} B$, asserting that $f_!$ is an enriched $\mathcal{D}(Y)$-linear module functor.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is relative purity and how is it measured by the relative dualizing object?
Hint
For a smooth morphism $f$ of relative dimension $d$, relative purity is the natural equivalence $f^!(-) \simeq f^*(-) \otimes f^!(\mathbf{1}) \simeq f^*(-)(d)[2d]$, identifying $f^!$ as a Tate-twisted shift of $f^*$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How do open covers give rise to Mayer-Vietoris exact triangles in six-functor formalisms?
Hint
For an open cover $X = U \cup V$ with intersection $W = U \cap V$, the localization sequences for open immersions glue to produce the distinguished triangle $C^*(X) \to C^*(U) \oplus C^*(V) \to C^*(W) \xrightarrow{+1}$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How is the homology of a closed subscheme $Z$ relative to $X$ defined?
Hint
As the Borel-Moore homology of the closed immersion $i \colon Z \hookrightarrow X$, computed by $C_*^{\mathrm{BM}}(Z) \simeq p_* i_* i^! p^!\mathbf{1} \simeq p_* i_! i^! \omega_X$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
Why can the localization axiom be difficult to establish in non-topological contexts (e.g., Kashiwara's lemma)?
Hint
Localization requires that for a closed immersion $i$, $i_*$ is fully faithful with left adjoint $i^*$; for $\mathcal{D}$-modules, this full faithfulness is Kashiwara's equivalence, which requires deep analytic/algebraic regularity theorems.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
How does the abstract blow-up square encode blow-up excision in cohomology via proper base change?
Hint
For a blow-up $\widetilde{X} \to X$ with center $Z$ and exceptional divisor $E$, the Cartesian square is an abstract cdh-distinguished square; proper base change and localization formally produce the excision fiber sequence $C^*(X) \to C^*(\widetilde{X}) \oplus C^*(Z) \to C^*(E) \xrightarrow{+1}$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is the Beck-Chevalley condition for a Cartesian square?
Hint
For a Cartesian square with projections $f, g, f', g'$, the natural transformation $g^* f_* \to f'_* g'^*$ (or $g^* f_! \to f'_! g'^*$) formed by adjunction units and counits is an isomorphism.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is proper base change vs. smooth base change?
Hint
Proper base change states $g^* f_* \xrightarrow{\sim} f'_* g'^*$ when $f$ is proper; smooth base change states $g'_! f'^! \xrightarrow{\sim} f^! g_!$ (and $g^* f_* \xrightarrow{\sim} f'_* g'^*$) when $g$ is smooth.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
Why does the pullback along a smooth morphism admit a left adjoint $p_\#$?
Hint
By relative purity, $p^*(-) \simeq p^!(-)(-d)[-2d]$; since $p^!$ is right adjoint to $p_!$, $p^*$ admits the left adjoint $p_\#(-) := p_!(-)(d)[2d]$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is a Nisnevich-Mayer-Vietoris square?
Hint
An elementary distinguished square where $U \hookrightarrow X$ is an open immersion, $V \to X$ is an étale morphism, and $(V \setminus V \times_X U) \to (X \setminus U)$ is an isomorphism; coefficient systems satisfy descent on these squares.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456

What are the axiomatic conditions defining a coefficient system in Gallauer's framework?
Hint

Hint
Any coefficient system $\mathcal{D}$ uniquely extends to a full six-functor formalism equipped with $(f^*, f_*, f_!, f^!, \otimes, \underline{\mathrm{Hom}})$, Grothendieck duality, proper base change, and the projection formula; morphisms of coefficient systems induce morphisms of six-functor formalisms.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456

How does Ind-completion resolve presentability issues for small coefficient systems?
Hint
By replacing a small category of constructible/dualizable sheaves $\mathcal{D}_c(X)$ with its Ind-completion $\mathrm{Ind}(\mathcal{D}_c(X)) \simeq \mathcal{D}(X)$, ensuring all limits, colimits, and adjoints exist via the Adjoint Functor Theorem.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456

Hint

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456

Hint

Hint

What characterizes an orientable coefficient system?
Hint

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
What is an exponential coefficient system (exponential motives) and its 7th operation?
Hint

Gallauer
Why does exceptional functoriality require the support property?
Hint
To guarantee that $f_!$ is independent of the choice of compactification $X \xrightarrow{j} \overline{X} \xrightarrow{p} Y$, the pushforward must vanish on the boundary complement, which is guaranteed by proper base change and localization.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer

Hint
$p^*(\mathbf{1})$ equips the space with constant coefficients; $p_*$ collects global sections, and its higher derived cohomology groups $R^i p_*$ quantify the homological obstructions to gluing local sections into global ones.

Gallauer
How are integral transforms and logical quantifiers realized in six-functor formalisms?
Hint
An integral kernel transform along a correspondence $X \xleftarrow{g} W \xrightarrow{f} Y$ is the functor $\Phi_K(-) = f_!(g^*(-) \otimes K)$; in logic, $f_!$ acts as the existential quantifier $\exists_f$ and $f_*$ acts as the universal quantifier $\forall_f$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456
Gallauer
Why does cohomology possess a ring structure (cup product) while homology possesses a coalgebra structure?
Hint

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.10456

Borcherds on quantum field theory.
What is Borcherds' "life cycle of a mathematical physicist" in perturbative quantum field theory?
Hint
(1) Write down a classical Lagrangian density $\mathcal{L}(\phi, \partial \phi)$; (2) form the Feynman path integral $Z = \int \mathcal{D}\phi \, e^{i \int \mathcal{L} dx}$; (3) expand perturbatively as a formal power series $\sum a_n \lambda^n$ where each coefficient $a_n$ is a sum of finite-dimensional Feynman integrals labeled by graphs; (4) observe that the loop integrals diverge (ultraviolet divergences); (5) introduce a regulator/cutoff $\epsilon > 0$ to make the integrals finite; (6) absorb divergences into $\epsilon$-dependent bare parameters (mass, coupling constants, field normalization) via the renormalization group; (7) observe that the $\epsilon$-independent renormalized coefficients $a_n$ are finite; (8) observe that the resulting renormalized perturbation series $\sum a_n \lambda^n$ still has zero radius of convergence (Dyson's divergence argument); (9) truncate the divergent asymptotic series at a finite order to compare with experimental measurements.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014
Borcherds on quantum field theory.
How does Borcherds resolve the non-existence of an infinite-dimensional translation-invariant Lebesgue measure in the path integral?
Hint
By treating the functional integral not as an analytical measure, but algebraically as a formal perturbative generating series of finite-dimensional Feynman amplitudes evaluated with cutoffs, quotiented by the group of finite renormalization transformations acting simultaneously on Lagrangians and cutoff functions.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014
Borcherds on quantum field theory.
What is the difference between ultraviolet (UV) divergences and the asymptotic divergence of the perturbation series?
Hint
UV divergences are local short-distance singularities in individual loop momentum integrals that are removed by regularizing and adding local counterterms to the Lagrangian; asymptotic divergence is the divergence of the sum $\sum a_n \lambda^n$ due to the factorial growth $a_n \sim n!$ of the number of Feynman diagrams, requiring Borel summation or non-perturbative completions rather than renormalization.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014

How are fundamental particles classified by spin and statistics in the Standard Model?
Hint
Matter fields are fermions with half-integer spin ($s = 1/2$, such as quarks, electrons, and neutrinos) governed by Grassmann/anticommuting variables and Fermi-Dirac statistics; force carriers are bosons with integer spin ($s = 1$ gauge bosons $\gamma, W^\pm, Z^0, g$ and $s = 0$ Higgs scalar) governed by symmetric variables and Bose-Einstein statistics.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014

How does Borcherds rigorously define the algebra of Lagrangian densities using polynomial differential operators?
Hint
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real spacetime ($V \cong \mathbb{R}^n$) and $W$ a finite-dimensional complex representation of abstract field values equipped with complex conjugation. Let $\mathrm{Diff}(V)$ be the polynomial ring of translation-invariant differential operators $\mathbb{C}[\partial_1, \dots, \partial_n]$. The space of field variables is $J(W) = \mathrm{Diff}(V) \otimes_\mathbb{C} W$, and a classical Lagrangian density $\mathcal{L}$ is an element of the symmetric algebra $\mathrm{Sym}^\bullet(J(W))$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014
Borcherds on quantum field theory.
How does the vibrating string Lagrangian on $\mathbb{R}^2$ produce the wave equation via Hamilton's principle?
Hint
Let $W \cong \mathbb{R}$ with coordinate $\phi(t, x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. The Lagrangian density is $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2} (\partial_t \phi)^2 - \frac{1}{2} (\partial_x \phi)^2$. Setting the variation of the action $\delta S = \delta \int \mathcal{L} \, dt\,dx = 0$ and applying integration by parts yields the Euler-Lagrange equation $\partial_t^2 \phi - \partial_x^2 \phi = 0$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014
Borcherds on quantum field theory.
How is the real scalar field generalized to $\phi^4$-theory on $\mathbb{R}^n$?
Hint
The Lagrangian density is $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2} \partial_\mu \phi \partial^\mu \phi - \frac{1}{2} m^2 \phi^2 - \frac{\lambda}{4!} \phi^4$, whose Euler-Lagrange equation is the non-linear Klein-Gordon equation $(\Box + m^2)\phi + \frac{\lambda}{3!} \phi^3 = 0$, where $\Box = \partial_\mu \partial^\mu$.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014
Borcherds on quantum field theory.
How is the conserved Noether current $j^\mu$ derived for a complex scalar field $\phi$?
Hint
For $\mathcal{L} = \partial_\mu \phi^* \partial^\mu \phi - m^2 \phi^* \phi$, global $\mathrm{U}(1)$-phase invariance $\phi \mapsto e^{i\alpha} \phi$ has infinitesimal generator $\delta \phi = i\phi, \delta \phi^* = -i\phi^*$. The resulting Noether current $j^\mu = i(\phi^* \partial^\mu \phi - \phi \partial^\mu \phi^*)$ satisfies the continuity equation $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ on shell (modulo the Euler-Lagrange ideal).
https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0204014

Why is the Noether current $j^\mu$ mathematically an $(n-1)$-form defined modulo exact forms?

Conserved currents integrate over spacelike $(n-1)$-dimensional hypersurfaces $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ to yield the conserved charge $Q = \int_\Sigma *j$; changing $j$ by an identically conserved term $\partial_\nu K^{[\mu\nu]}$ alters $j$ by the exterior derivative $d(*K)$ of an $(n-2)$-form, so Noether currents canonically represent cohomology classes in $\Omega^{n-1}(V) / d\Omega^{n-2}(V)$.

The gauge potential $A = A_\mu dx^\mu$ has curvature $F = dA = \frac{1}{2} F_{\mu\nu} dx^\mu \wedge dx^\nu$ where $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$. The Maxwell Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{4} F_{\mu\nu} F^{\mu\nu}$ yields the Euler-Lagrange equation $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = 0$, which expresses the cocycle condition $d * F = 0$ in the de Rham complex.

Hint

When is an $\mathcal{O}_X$-module coherent?
Hint
An $\mathcal{O}_X$-module $\mathcal{F}$ is coherent if it is of finite type and for every open $U$ and morphism $\mathcal{O}_U^n \to \mathcal{F}|_U$, the kernel is of finite type; on locally Noetherian schemes, coherence is equivalent to being quasi-coherent and locally of finite type.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is a constructible set in a Noetherian topological space?
Hint
A finite disjoint union of locally closed subsets (intersections of open and closed sets); equivalently, a subset in the Boolean algebra generated by open sets.

How is the degree of a point, a map, and a line bundle defined on a projective curve $C$?
Hint
The degree of a closed point $p$ is $[k(p):k]$; the degree of a finite map $\pi \colon C \to C'$ is the rank of $\pi_* \mathcal{O}_C$; the degree of a line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ is $\deg(\mathcal{L}) = \chi(C, \mathcal{L}) - \chi(C, \mathcal{O}_C)$, matching $\sum n_i [k(p_i):k]$ for $\mathcal{L} \cong \mathcal{O}_C(\sum n_i p_i)$.

What is a dualizing sheaf for a proper $k$-scheme $X$ of dimension $n$?
Hint
A coherent sheaf $\omega_X$ equipped with a trace map $\mathrm{Tr} \colon H^n(X, \omega_X) \to k$ inducing the Serre duality isomorphism $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\mathcal{F}, \omega_X) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^n(X, \mathcal{F})^\vee$ for all coherent sheaves $\mathcal{F}$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

When is a morphism of schemes étale?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ that is flat and unramified (formally étale and locally of finite presentation), equivalently smooth of relative dimension $0$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is the Euler characteristic $\chi(X, \mathcal{F})$ of a coherent sheaf?
Hint
The alternating sum of the dimensions of its cohomology spaces $\chi(X, \mathcal{F}) := \sum_{i=0}^{\dim X} (-1)^i \dim_k H^i(X, \mathcal{F})$.

What is the extension by zero functor $j_!$ for an open immersion $j \colon U \hookrightarrow X$?
Hint
The exact functor $j_! \colon \mathbf{Sh}(U) \to \mathbf{Sh}(X)$ defined as the sheafification of $V \mapsto \mathcal{F}(V)$ if $V \subset U$ and $0$ otherwise; it is the left adjoint to the restriction/pullback functor $j^*$.

When is a scheme factorial and what does it imply about normalities?
Hint
A scheme $X$ is factorial if all its local rings $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ are unique factorization domains (UFDs); since UFDs are integrally closed, every factorial scheme is normal and its Weil divisors coincide with Cartier divisors.

Algebraic geometry definitions.
When is a morphism of schemes faithfully flat?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ that is flat ($\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a flat $\mathcal{O}_{Y, f(x)}$-module for all $x$) and surjective on underlying topological spaces.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is the fiber and the generic fiber of a morphism $f \colon X \to Y$?
Hint
The fiber over $y \in Y$ is the fiber product $X_y := X \times_Y \mathrm{Spec}(k(y))$; if $Y$ is integral with generic point $\eta$, the generic fiber is $X_\eta := X \times_Y \mathrm{Spec}(K(Y))$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

When is a morphism finite, locally of finite type, and locally of finite presentation?
Hint
Finite if affine and $\mathcal{O}_X(f^{-1}(U))$ is a finitely generated module over $\mathcal{O}_Y(U)$; locally of finite type if $\mathcal{O}_X(f^{-1}(U))$ is a finitely generated algebra; locally of finite presentation if $\mathcal{O}_X(f^{-1}(U))$ is a finitely presented algebra.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a flasque (flabby) sheaf?
Hint
A sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ such that for every open inclusion $V \subset U$, the restriction map $\mathcal{F}(U) \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{F}(V)$ is surjective; flasque sheaves are acyclic for the global section functor $\Gamma(X, -)$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
When is a coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ locally free of rank $r$?
Hint
When $X$ admits an open covering $\{U_i\}$ such that $\mathcal{F}|_{U_i} \cong \mathcal{O}_{U_i}^{\oplus r}$; locally free sheaves of rank $r$ correspond bijectively to algebraic vector bundles of rank $r$.

What is the geometric genus and the arithmetic genus of a smooth projective variety $X$?
Hint
Geometric genus is $p_g(X) := \dim_k H^0(X, \omega_X) = \dim_k H^n(X, \mathcal{O}_X)$; arithmetic genus is $p_a(X) := (-1)^n (\chi(X, \mathcal{O}_X) - 1)$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is the Hilbert polynomial $P_{\mathcal{F}}(m)$ of a coherent sheaf on $\mathbb{P}_k^n$?
Hint
The polynomial that for $m \gg 0$ equals the Euler characteristic $P_{\mathcal{F}}(m) = \chi(X, \mathcal{F}(m)) = \dim_k H^0(X, \mathcal{F}(m))$; its leading coefficient gives $(\dim X)! \cdot \deg(X)$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is an injective object and an injective resolution in an abelian category?
Hint
An object $I$ such that $\mathrm{Hom}(-, I)$ is an exact functor; an injective resolution of $A$ is an exact sequence $0 \to A \to I^0 \to I^1 \to I^2 \to \dots$ with each $I^k$ injective, used to compute right derived functors $R^i F(A) = H^i(F(I^\bullet))$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

When is a morphism integral and what is a normal scheme?
Hint
An affine morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ where every local ring extension $\mathcal{O}_Y(U) \to \mathcal{O}_X(f^{-1}(U))$ is an integral ring extension; a scheme is normal if all its local rings $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ are integrally closed domains (satisfying Serre's conditions $R_1 + S_2$).

What is the module of relative Kähler differentials $\Omega_{X/Y}^1$?
Hint
The quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_X$-module generated locally by symbols $df$ ($f \in \mathcal{O}_X$) satisfying $d(f+g) = df+dg$, $d(fg) = f\,dg + g\,df$, and $d(h) = 0$ for $h \in \mathcal{O}_Y$; equivalently defined via the diagonal conormal sheaf $\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2$ on $X \times_Y X$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is a locally closed embedding and a normal bundle?
Hint
A morphism factoring as a closed embedding into an open subscheme $X \hookrightarrow U \subset Y$; for a closed embedding $i \colon X \hookrightarrow Y$ cut out by ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}$, the conormal sheaf is $\mathcal{N}_{X/Y}^* = \mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2$ and the normal bundle is its dual $\mathcal{N}_{X/Y} = (\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2)^\vee$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is the Picard group $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$?
Hint
The abelian group of isomorphism classes of invertible sheaves (line bundles) on $X$ under the tensor product operation $\mathcal{L} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{M}$, with identity $\mathcal{O}_X$ and inverse $\mathcal{L}^\vee = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{O}_X)$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
When is a morphism of schemes proper?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ that is separated, of finite type, and universally closed (meaning for every base change $Y' \to Y$, the map $X \times_Y Y' \to Y'$ is closed in the Zariski topology).
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
When is a morphism of schemes separated?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ whose diagonal morphism $\Delta_{X/Y} \colon X \to X \times_Y X$ is a closed embedding, formalizing the Hausdorff separation property in algebraic geometry.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is a quasi-coherent sheaf vs. a coherent sheaf?
Hint
An $\mathcal{O}_X$-module $\mathcal{F}$ is quasi-coherent if it is locally presented as the cokernel of a map between free $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules $\mathcal{O}_X^{\oplus I} \to \mathcal{O}_X^{\oplus J} \to \mathcal{F} \to 0$; it is coherent if the indexing sets $I, J$ can be chosen finite locally.

What is the Zariski tangent space and cotangent space at a point $p \in X$?
Hint
The Zariski cotangent space is $\mathfrak{m}_p / \mathfrak{m}_p^2$ over the residue field $k(p) = \mathcal{O}_{X, p}/\mathfrak{m}_p$; the Zariski tangent space is its linear dual $T_p X = (\mathfrak{m}_p / \mathfrak{m}_p^2)^* = \mathrm{Der}_k(\mathcal{O}_{X, p}, k(p))$.

When is a scheme smooth over a field $k$ of dimension $d$?
Hint
When $X$ is locally of finite presentation over $k$, flat, and its module of Kähler differentials $\Omega_{X/k}^1$ is a locally free $\mathcal{O}_X$-module of rank $d$; equivalently, when all geometric fibers are regular local rings.

What is a Weil divisor and when does it define a line bundle $\mathcal{O}(D)$?
Hint
A formal integer linear combination $D = \sum n_i Y_i$ of codimension 1 irreducible closed subvarieties $Y_i$ on a Noetherian integral separated scheme regular in codimension 1; on a locally factorial scheme, every Weil divisor is Cartier and defines an invertible sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X(D)$.

What is a regular local ring and a regular embedding of schemes?
Hint
A Noetherian local ring $(A, \mathfrak{m})$ is regular if $\dim_{k} \mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2 = \dim(A)$; a closed embedding $i \colon X \hookrightarrow Y$ is regular of codimension $r$ if its defining ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}$ is locally generated by a regular sequence of length $r$, making $\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2$ locally free of rank $r$.

What are the Veronese and Segre embeddings?
Hint
The Veronese embedding $\nu_d \colon \mathbb{P}^n \to \mathbb{P}^{\binom{n+d}{n}-1}$ is given by all degree-$d$ monomials, proving $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(d)$ is very ample; the Segre embedding $\sigma \colon \mathbb{P}^n \times \mathbb{P}^m \to \mathbb{P}^{(n+1)(m+1)-1}$ is given by products of coordinates $([x_i], [y_j]) \mapsto [x_i y_j]$, realizing product varieties as closed projective subschemes.

What is the derived category $\mathcal{D}(X)$ and the $\infty$-category $\mathbf{QCoh}(X)$ in higher algebraic geometry?
Hint
$\mathcal{D}(X) = \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{QCoh}(X))$ is the stable $\infty$-category obtained by inverting quasi-isomorphisms; for an affine derived scheme $\mathbf{Spec}(A)$ with $A \in \mathbf{CAlg}$, $\mathbf{QCoh}(\mathbf{Spec}(A)) \simeq \mathbf{Mod}_A$ in the $\infty$-categorical sense.

What is a simplicial commutative ring and an $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring in derived algebraic geometry?
Hint
A simplicial commutative ring $A \in \mathbf{sCAlg}_k$ is a simplicial object in commutative $k$-algebras modeling connective derived commutative algebras; an $\mathbb{E}_\infty$-ring spectrum $A \in \mathbf{CAlg}(\mathbf{Sp})$ is a strictly commutative ring object in spectra, generalizing rings to arbitrary virtual/non-connective cohomological degrees.

What is the cotangent complex $\mathbb{L}_{X/Y}$ of a morphism in derived algebraic geometry?
Hint
The left derived functor of the Kähler differentials functor $\mathbb{L}_{X/Y} \in \mathbf{QCoh}(X)$; its degree $0$ cohomology computes the classical Kähler differentials $H^0(\mathbb{L}_{X/Y}) \cong \Omega_{\pi_0(X)/\pi_0(Y)}^1$ and its negative cohomology groups $H^{-i}(\mathbb{L}_{X/Y})$ capture obstruction theories and non-transverse derived intersections.

What is a quasi-smooth morphism and a derived local complete intersection?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ locally of finite presentation between derived schemes/stacks whose relative cotangent complex $\mathbb{L}_{X/Y}$ has Tor-amplitude concentrated in $[-1, 0]$; it carries an intrinsic virtual fundamental class of virtual dimension $\mathrm{virdim}(f) = \mathrm{rank}(H^0(\mathbb{L}_{X/Y})) - \mathrm{rank}(H^{-1}(\mathbb{L}_{X/Y}))$.

What is an algebraic stack and a derived Artin stack?
Hint
A classical algebraic/Artin stack is a 1-sheaf of groupoids with a smooth atlas $U \to \mathcal{X}$ from a scheme; a derived Artin stack is an $\infty$-sheaf of spaces $\mathcal{X} \colon \mathbf{CAlg}_k^{\mathrm{cn}} \to \mathcal{S}$ admitting a smooth surjective atlas $U \to \mathcal{X}$ from a derived scheme, with an obstruction theory controlled by its global cotangent complex $\mathbb{L}_{\mathcal{X}}$.

What is a perfect complex in higher algebra?
Hint
An object $E \in \mathbf{QCoh}(X)$ that is compact and dualizable in the symmetric monoidal stable $\infty$-category $\mathbf{QCoh}(X)$; on a classical scheme it is locally quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of algebraic vector bundles.

What is the derived loop space $\mathcal{L}X$ and its relation to Hochschild homology?
Hint
The derived mapping stack $\mathcal{L}X := \mathbf{Map}(S^1, X) \simeq X \times_{X \times X}^{\mathbf{R}} X$; by the HKR theorem, functions on the derived loop space compute the Hochschild homology $\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}X) \simeq \mathbf{HH}_*(X)$.

What is a shifted symplectic structure on a derived Artin stack?
Hint
In the sense of Pantev-Toën-Vaquié-Vezzosi (PTVV), an $n$-shifted symplectic structure on a derived stack $X$ is a non-degenerate, closed 2-form $\omega \in \mathrm{Sym}^2(\mathbb{T}_X[-n])$ of degree $n$, generalizing classical symplectic structures ($n=0$) and lagrangian intersection structures ($n=-1$).

What is a stable $\infty$-category?
Hint
An $\infty$-category $\mathcal{C}$ that has a zero object, admits all finite limits and colimits, and where a square is a pushout square if and only if it is a pullback square, formalizing triangulated categories equipped with functorial shifts $\Sigma$ and canonical fiber/cofiber sequences.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf

What is the t-structure on a stable $\infty$-category?
Hint
A pair of full subcategories $(\mathcal{C}_{\ge 0}, \mathcal{C}_{\le 0})$ satisfying $\mathrm{Map}(X, Y) \simeq *$ for $X \in \mathcal{C}_{\ge 1}, Y \in \mathcal{C}_{\le 0}$ and producing canonical truncation fiber sequences $\tau_{\ge 0} X \to X \to \tau_{\le -1} X$; its heart $\mathcal{C}^\heartsuit = \mathcal{C}_{\ge 0} \cap \mathcal{C}_{\le 0}$ is an ordinary abelian category.

What is a presheaf of sets on a topological space $X$?
Hint
A contravariant functor $\mathcal{F} \colon \mathbf{Open}(X)^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{Set}$ assigning to each open set $U \subset X$ a set of sections $\mathcal{F}(U)$, and to each inclusion $V \subset U$ a restriction map $\mathrm{res}_{U,V} \colon \mathcal{F}(U) \to \mathcal{F}(V)$ satisfying $\mathrm{res}_{U,U} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{F}(U)}$ and $\mathrm{res}_{V,W} \circ \mathrm{res}_{U,V} = \mathrm{res}_{U,W}$.

What is a sheaf of sets on a topological space $X$?
Hint
A presheaf $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying two axioms for every open cover $U = \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$: (1) Locality/Separation: if $s, t \in \mathcal{F}(U)$ satisfy $s|_{U_i} = t|_{U_i}$ for all $i$, then $s = t$; (2) Gluing: if sections $s_i \in \mathcal{F}(U_i)$ satisfy $s_i|_{U_i \cap U_j} = s_j|_{U_i \cap U_j}$ for all $i, j$, there exists a unique $s \in \mathcal{F}(U)$ such that $s|_{U_i} = s_i$.

What is the stalk of a presheaf $\mathcal{F}$ at a point $x \in X$?
Hint
The filtered colimit $\mathcal{F}_x := \varinjlim_{U \ni x} \mathcal{F}(U)$ over all open neighborhoods containing $x$, whose elements are germs $\langle U, s \rangle_x$ modulo the equivalence relation $\langle U, s \rangle \sim \langle V, t \rangle \iff \exists W \subset U \cap V$ containing $x$ with $s|_W = t|_W$.

What is the sheafification $\mathcal{F}^+$ of a presheaf $\mathcal{F}$?
Hint
The sheaf $\mathcal{F}^+(U) := \{ s \colon U \to \coprod_{x \in U} \mathcal{F}_x \mid \forall x \in U, s(x) \in \mathcal{F}_x \text{ and } s \text{ is locally matched by sections of } \mathcal{F} \}$; it is the left adjoint to the forgetful inclusion functor $\mathbf{Sh}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{PSh}(X)$.

What is a locally ringed space?
Hint
A pair $(X, \mathcal{O}_X)$ where $X$ is a topological space and $\mathcal{O}_X$ is a sheaf of rings such that for every point $x \in X$, the stalk $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a local ring (possesses a unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}_x$).

What is a morphism of locally ringed spaces $(f, f^\sharp) \colon (X, \mathcal{O}_X) \to (Y, \mathcal{O}_Y)$?
Hint
A continuous map $f \colon X \to Y$ together with a sheaf homomorphism $f^\sharp \colon \mathcal{O}_Y \to f_* \mathcal{O}_X$ such that for every $x \in X$, the induced stalk map $f_x^\sharp \colon \mathcal{O}_{Y, f(x)} \to \mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a local ring homomorphism (satisfying $(f_x^\sharp)^{-1}(\mathfrak{m}_x) = \mathfrak{m}_{f(x)}$).

What is the prime spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}(A)$ of a commutative ring $A$?
Hint

What is a distinguished open set $D(f)$ in $\mathrm{Spec}(A)$?
Hint
The basic open set $D(f) := \mathrm{Spec}(A) \setminus V(f) = \{\mathfrak{p} \in \mathrm{Spec}(A) \mid f \notin \mathfrak{p}\}$, which is canonically isomorphic to the affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec}(A_f)$.

What is a scheme?
Hint
A locally ringed space $(X, \mathcal{O}_X)$ that admits an open cover $\{U_i\}$ such that each open subspace $(U_i, \mathcal{O}_X|_{U_i})$ is isomorphic as a locally ringed space to an affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec}(A_i)$.

What is the sheaf $\widetilde{M}$ associated to an $A$-module $M$ on $\mathrm{Spec}(A)$?

The quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec}(A)}$-module whose sections on basic opens are $\widetilde{M}(D(f)) = M_f$ and whose stalks are $\widetilde{M}_\mathfrak{p} = M_\mathfrak{p}$; the functor $M \mapsto \widetilde{M}$ defines an equivalence of categories between $A\mathbf{-Mod}$ and $\mathbf{QCoh}(\mathrm{Spec}(A))$.

What is the homogeneous spectrum $\mathrm{Proj}(S_\bullet)$ of a $\mathbb{N}$-graded ring $S_\bullet$?

What is the Serre twisting sheaf $\mathcal{O}_X(n)$ on $X = \mathrm{Proj}(S_\bullet)$?

What is an open immersion of schemes?
Hint
A morphism of schemes $f \colon U \to X$ that is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset $V \subset X$ and induces an isomorphism of sheaves $\mathcal{O}_X|_V \xrightarrow{\sim} f_* \mathcal{O}_U$.

What is the scheme-theoretic image of a morphism $f \colon X \to Y$?
Hint
The unique smallest closed subscheme $Z \subset Y$ through which $f$ factors; locally on $\mathrm{Spec}(B) \subset Y$ with $f^{-1}(\mathrm{Spec}(B)) = \mathrm{Spec}(A)$, it is defined by the ideal $\ker(B \to A)$.

What is the scheme-theoretic closure of a subscheme $W \subset X$?
Hint
The scheme-theoretic image of the immersion morphism $i \colon W \hookrightarrow X$, corresponding to the smallest closed subscheme containing $W$.

What is the reduction $X_{\mathrm{red}}$ of a scheme $X$?
Hint
The closed subscheme cut out by the nilradical ideal sheaf $\mathcal{N} = \sqrt{(0)} \subset \mathcal{O}_X$; it has the same underlying topological space as $X$ and its stalks are the reduced local rings $\mathcal{O}_{X, x} / \mathrm{Nil}(\mathcal{O}_{X, x})$.

What is the dimension and codimension of a scheme $X$?
Hint
The Krull dimension $\dim(X)$ is the supremum of lengths $n$ of chains of irreducible closed subsets $Z_0 \subsetneq Z_1 \subsetneq \dots \subsetneq Z_n \subset X$; the codimension $\mathrm{codim}(Y, X)$ of an irreducible closed subset $Y$ is the supremum of lengths of chains $Y = Z_0 \subsetneq Z_1 \subsetneq \dots \subsetneq Z_k \subset X$.

What is a regular sequence on a module $M$?
Hint
A sequence of elements $x_1, \dots, x_r \in A$ such that $x_1$ is not a zero-divisor on $M$, and for each $i \in \{2, \dots, r\}$, $x_i$ is not a zero-divisor on $M / (x_1, \dots, x_{i-1})M$, with $M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M \neq 0$.

What is the depth of a local ring $(A, \mathfrak{m})$ on a module $M$?
Hint
The maximal length of an $M$-regular sequence with elements in the maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$, denoted $\mathrm{depth}(M) = \min \{ i \ge 0 \mid \mathrm{Ext}_A^i(A/\mathfrak{m}, M) \neq 0 \}$.

What is a Cohen-Macaulay scheme?
Hint
A locally Noetherian scheme $X$ whose local rings $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ satisfy $\mathrm{depth}(\mathcal{O}_{X, x}) = \dim(\mathcal{O}_{X, x})$ for all $x \in X$.

Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a Gorenstein scheme?
Hint
A Cohen-Macaulay locally Noetherian scheme $X$ whose local rings $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ have finite injective dimension as modules over themselves (equivalently, the canonical module $\omega_{\mathcal{O}_{X, x}}$ is an invertible module of rank 1).
