What are Serre's conditions $R_k$ and $S_k$?
Hint
A Noetherian ring $A$ satisfies: (1) $R_k$ (Regular in codimension $\le k$) if $A_\mathfrak{p}$ is a regular local ring for all $\mathfrak{p}$ with $\mathrm{height}(\mathfrak{p}) \le k$; (2) $S_k$ (Serre's depth condition) if $\mathrm{depth}(A_\mathfrak{p}) \ge \min(k, \mathrm{dim}(A_\mathfrak{p}))$ for all $\mathfrak{p}$. Serre's Criterion states: $A$ is reduced $\iff R_0 + S_1$, and $A$ is normal $\iff R_1 + S_2$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the normalization of an integral scheme $X$ in a field extension $L$ of its function field $K(X)$?
Hint
The unique normal scheme $\widetilde{X}$ equipped with a dominant morphism $\pi \colon \widetilde{X} \to X$ such that for every affine open $\mathrm{Spec}(A) \subset X$, $\pi^{-1}(\mathrm{Spec}(A)) = \mathrm{Spec}(A')$, where $A'$ is the integral closure of $A$ in $L$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a local complete intersection (lci) morphism?
Hint
A morphism of schemes $f \colon X \to Y$ that factors locally as a regular closed embedding $i \colon X \hookrightarrow P$ followed by a smooth morphism $p \colon P \to Y$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a flat module and a flat morphism?
Hint
An $A$-module $M$ is flat if the functor $- \otimes_A M$ is exact on $A\mathbf{-Mod}$; a morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ is flat if for all $x \in X$, $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a flat $\mathcal{O}_{Y, f(x)}$-module via $f_x^\sharp$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is an unramified morphism?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ locally of finite presentation such that for every $x \in X$, $\mathfrak{m}_{f(x)} \mathcal{O}_{X, x} = \mathfrak{m}_x$ and the residue field extension $k(x) / k(f(x))$ is finite and separable; equivalently, the relative Kähler differentials vanish: $\Omega_{X/Y}^1 = 0$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a smooth morphism of relative dimension $d$?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ that is flat, locally of finite presentation, and whose geometric fibers $X_{\overline{y}} := X \times_Y \mathrm{Spec}(\overline{k(y)})$ are smooth varieties of pure dimension $d$ over $\overline{k(y)}$ (equivalently, $\Omega_{X/Y}^1$ is locally free of rank $d$ and $f$ satisfies infinitesimal lifting).
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is formal smoothness, formal etaleness, and formal unramifiedness (Infinitesimal Lifting Criterion)?
Hint
For every commutative ring $A$ and square-zero ideal $I \subset A$ ($I^2 = 0$), the map $\mathrm{Hom}_Y(\mathrm{Spec}(A), X) \to \mathrm{Hom}_Y(\mathrm{Spec}(A/I), X)$ is: (1) surjective if $f$ is formally smooth; (2) bijective if $f$ is formally étale; (3) injective if $f$ is formally unramified.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a valuative criterion of separatedness?
Hint
A morphism of finite type $f \colon X \to Y$ between Noetherian schemes is separated if and only if for every valuation ring $R$ with fraction field $K$, and every commutative diagram $\mathrm{Spec}(K) \to X$, $\mathrm{Spec}(R) \to Y$, there exists at most one lift $\mathrm{Spec}(R) \to X$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a valuative criterion of properness?
Hint
A morphism of finite type $f \colon X \to Y$ between Noetherian schemes is proper if and only if for every valuation ring $R$ with fraction field $K$, and every commutative diagram $\mathrm{Spec}(K) \to X$, $\mathrm{Spec}(R) \to Y$, there exists a unique lift $\mathrm{Spec}(R) \to X$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a projective morphism of schemes?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ that factors as a closed embedding $i \colon X \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}_Y^n = \mathbb{P}_{\mathbb{Z}}^n \times_{\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})} Y$ followed by the canonical projection $\mathbb{P}_Y^n \to Y$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a quasi-projective morphism?
Hint
A morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ that factors as an open immersion $j \colon X \hookrightarrow \overline{X}$ into a scheme $\overline{X}$ that is projective over $Y$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is an invertible sheaf (algebraic line bundle)?
Hint
A locally free $\mathcal{O}_X$-module $\mathcal{L}$ of rank 1, meaning $X$ is covered by open sets $U$ on which $\mathcal{L}|_U \cong \mathcal{O}_U$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the transition function cocycle of a locally free sheaf?
Hint
For a trivializing open cover $\{U_i\}$ with isomorphisms $\psi_i \colon \mathcal{F}|_{U_i} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{O}_{U_i}^r$, the transition functions are $g_{ij} = \psi_i \circ \psi_j^{-1} \in \mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal{O}_X(U_i \cap U_j))$, satisfying the 1-cocycle condition $g_{ij} g_{jk} = g_{ik}$ on $U_i \cap U_j \cap U_k$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the dual sheaf $\mathcal{F}^\vee$ and internal Hom $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{G})$?
Hint
$\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{G})$ is the sheaf $U \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_U}(\mathcal{F}|_U, \mathcal{G}|_U)$; the dual sheaf is $\mathcal{F}^\vee := \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{O}_X)$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the dualizing complex $\omega_X^\bullet$ on a Noetherian scheme?
Hint
An object $\omega_X^\bullet \in D_c^b(X)$ of finite injective dimension such that the natural biduality evaluation map $\mathcal{F} \to \mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathbf{R}\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathcal{F}, \omega_X^\bullet), \omega_X^\bullet)$ is a quasi-isomorphism for all $\mathcal{F} \in D_c^b(X)$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is Serre duality for smooth projective varieties?
Hint
For a smooth projective variety $X$ of dimension $n$ over a field $k$ with canonical bundle $\omega_X = \bigwedge^n \Omega_{X/k}^1$, there is a canonical trace map $\mathrm{Tr} \colon H^n(X, \omega_X) \xrightarrow{\sim} k$ inducing perfect pairings $H^i(X, \mathcal{F}) \times \mathrm{Ext}^{n-i}(\mathcal{F}, \omega_X) \to k$ for every coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the Riemann-Roch Theorem for smooth projective curves?
Hint
For an invertible sheaf $\mathcal{L} \cong \mathcal{O}_C(D)$ on a smooth projective curve $C$ of genus $g$ over $k$: $\dim_k H^0(C, \mathcal{L}) - \dim_k H^1(C, \mathcal{L}) = \deg(\mathcal{L}) + 1 - g$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the Riemann-Hurwitz Formula for a finite separable morphism $\pi \colon C \to C'$ of curves?
Hint
$2g(C) - 2 = \deg(\pi)(2g(C') - 2) + \deg(R)$, where $R = \sum_{p \in C} (e_p - 1) p$ is the ramification divisor and $e_p$ is the ramification index at $p$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the blow-up $\mathrm{Bl}_Z(X)$ of a scheme $X$ along a closed subscheme $Z$?
Hint
If $Z \subset X$ is cut out by the ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{O}_X$, the blow-up is the scheme $\mathrm{Bl}_Z(X) := \mathrm{Proj}_X\left(\bigoplus_{d \ge 0} \mathcal{I}^d\right)$ equipped with the canonical projection $\pi \colon \mathrm{Bl}_Z(X) \to X$; the preimage $E = \pi^{-1}(Z) \cong \mathrm{Proj}_Z\left(\bigoplus_{d \ge 0} \mathcal{I}^d / \mathcal{I}^{d+1}\right)$ is an effective Cartier divisor called the exceptional divisor.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is a linear system $|D|$ and a complete linear system on a variety $X$?
Hint
The complete linear system of an effective divisor $D$ is the projective space $|D| := \mathbb{P}(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(D))) = \{ D' \ge 0 \mid D' \sim D \}$; a linear system $\mathfrak{d} \subset |D|$ is a projective linear subspace corresponding to a vector subspace $V \subset H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(D))$.
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Algebraic geometry definitions.
What is the Grassmannian variety $\mathbf{Gr}(k, V)$?
Hint
The projective scheme representing the functor that assigns to any scheme $S$ the set of rank-$k$ locally free quotient sheaves of $V \otimes_k \mathcal{O}_S$ (or rank-$k$ sub-bundles of $V$).
https://c-keyes.github.io/files/definitions.pdf
Slide 2 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How did Newton historically introduce operator-theoretic ideas into mechanics?
Hint
By replacing static geometric variables with fluxions and differential operators acting on functions, anticipating the operational formalism of quantum observables.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 5 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why does quantum mechanics provide a more subtle answer to the nature of space and the reduction of the wave packet?
Hint
The collapse of the wave packet is an irreversible thermodynamic phenomenon; observables are non-commuting operators on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, meaning quantum states interact non-trivially with the algebra of observables.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 8 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does physical time emerge from quantum thermodynamics and thermal equilibrium?
Hint
A thermal equilibrium state at inverse temperature $\beta$ is given by the Gibbs state $\varphi(A) = \frac{\mathrm{Tr}(A e^{-\beta H})}{\mathrm{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})}$; time evolution $A \mapsto \sigma_t(A) = e^{i t H} A e^{-i t H}$ is uniquely determined by the algebraic KMS condition satisfied by $\varphi$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 10 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
State the Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) condition at inverse temperature $\beta$
Hint
A faithful state $\varphi$ on a von Neumann algebra $M$ satisfies the $\mathrm{KMS}_\beta$ condition with respect to a 1-parameter automorphism group $\sigma_t$ if for all $x, y \in M$, there exists a bounded holomorphic function $F(z)$ on the strip $0 \le \mathrm{Im}(z) \le \beta$ such that $F(t) = \varphi(x \sigma_t(y))$ and $F(t + i\beta) = \varphi(\sigma_t(y) x)$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 12 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
State the Tomita-Takesaki Theorem for von Neumann algebras
Hint
Let $M$ be a von Neumann algebra and $\varphi$ a faithful normal state on $M$. There exists a unique 1-parameter group of automorphisms $\sigma_t^\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(M)$ (the modular automorphism group) fulfilling the $\mathrm{KMS}_1$ condition with respect to $\varphi$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 13 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How did Connes' thesis establish that a von Neumann algebra possesses a canonical thermodynamic time evolution?
Hint
Connes proved the Radon-Nikodym cocycle theorem: for any two faithful normal states $\varphi, \psi$, the modular automorphism groups $\sigma_t^\varphi$ and $\sigma_t^\psi$ differ only by inner automorphisms $\mathrm{Ad}(u_t)$, yielding a canonical outer automorphism homomorphism $\delta \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathrm{Out}(M) = \mathrm{Aut}(M)/\mathrm{Inn}(M)$ independent of the state.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 15 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How is time evolution interpreted algebraically in quantum gravity?
Hint
Time is not an external geometric parameter but the canonical 1-parameter group of outer automorphisms $\delta \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{M})$ of the non-commutative von Neumann algebra of gravitational observables.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 17 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why does the spectrum of the Laplacian fail to characterize a compact Riemannian manifold?
Hint
John Milnor constructed non-isometric 16-dimensional flat tori that are isospectral ($\mathrm{Spec}(\Delta_1) = \mathrm{Spec}(\Delta_2)$), proving that one cannot "hear the shape of a drum" from the eigenvalue spectrum alone.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 19 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
What missing operator-theoretic information is needed beyond the spectrum to reconstruct a manifold?
Hint
The relative position (commutation relations) of two abelian von Neumann algebras acting on the Hilbert space $L^2(M)$: the algebra of smooth coordinates $C^\infty(M)$ and the algebra of momentum operators/differential operators generated by the Dirac operator $D$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 21 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does von Neumann's theorem characterize the algebra of bounded measurable functions on Hilbert space?
Hint
By von Neumann's uniqueness theorem, the maximal abelian $*$-algebra $L^\infty(M)$ acting by multiplication on $L^2(M)$ is uniquely isomorphic to the standard measure algebra of $M$, containing purely measure-theoretic, non-metric data.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 23 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why is the Dirac operator $D$ used instead of the scalar Laplacian $\Delta$?
Hint
The Dirac operator $D$ is a first-order differential operator providing a square root of the Laplacian ($D^2 = \Delta + \frac{1}{4}R$ via Lichnerowicz), whose inverse $D^{-1}$ represents the fermion propagator and directly encodes the metric and spin structure.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 25 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
What are the CKM invariant, $\mathrm{Spec}(D)$, and the relative spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}_N(M)$?
Hint
$\mathrm{Spec}(D)$ gives the energy levels/frequencies of the system, while the relative spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}_N(M)$ measures the relative modular position of $M$ inside $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$, encoding cross-correlations and transition probabilities between frequencies.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 27 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How is the Riemannian geodesic distance defined spectrally in noncommutative geometry?
Hint
Connes' spectral distance formula replaces the infimum of arc lengths by the dual operator formula: $d(p, q) = \sup \{ |f(p) - f(q)| : f \in C^\infty(M), \|[D, f]\| \le 1 \}$, where the infinitesimal line element is $ds = D^{-1}$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 29 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does noncommutative geometry describe spacetime unification in the Standard Model?
Hint
Spacetime is modeled as an almost-commutative spectral triple $(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{H}, D)$ with algebra $\mathcal{A} = C^\infty(M) \otimes \mathcal{A}_F$, where $\mathcal{A}_F = \mathbb{C} \oplus \mathbb{H} \oplus M_3(\mathbb{C})$ corresponds to the finite non-commutative geometry of the Standard Model.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 31 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
Why is the group of inner automorphisms $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{A})$ of $\mathcal{A} = C^\infty(M) \otimes M_n(\mathbb{C})$ identified with gauge transformations?
Hint
The automorphism group splits as a semi-direct product $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{A}) = \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{A}) \rtimes \mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{A})$, where $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{A}) \cong \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ gives gravity (diffeomorphisms) and $\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{A}) \cong C^\infty(M, \mathrm{SU}(n))$ gives the local internal gauge group.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 34 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does the shift from 4 to 10 dimensions arise in noncommutative geometry compared to string theory compactifications?
Hint
In string theory, 6 extra dimensions are compactified on an unnaturally small Calabi-Yau manifold; in NCG, the KO-dimension of the finite spectral triple $\mathcal{A}_F$ is $6 \pmod 8$, making the total metric/KO-dimension of spacetime $4 + 6 = 10 \equiv 2 \pmod 8$ without requiring geometric compactification.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf
Slide 37 Introduction to the Spectral Action Principle
How does the Spectral Action Principle unify gravity with the Standard Model forces?
Hint
The full bosonic action is given by the spectral action $\mathrm{Tr}(f(D_A / \Lambda)) + \frac{1}{2}\langle J\psi, D_A \psi\rangle$, where $D_A = D + A + \epsilon J A J^{-1}$ is the Dirac operator with gauge fluctuations; its asymptotic heat kernel expansion automatically produces the Einstein-Hilbert action, the Yang-Mills gauge actions, and the Higgs potential with unified coupling relations at the unification scale $\Lambda$.
http://cmtp.uniroma2.it/13MQP/slides/Connes.pdf

Why are physical systems frequently linearized?

How does one compute the partition function of a topological four-functor field theory?
Hint
A functor from the category of $d$-dimensional cobordisms; the partition function is the value of the functor on a $d$-torus, i.e. $Z(T)$. The partition function is the trace over the value of the QFT on the cylinder given by cutting, so the name comes from the cylinder cobordism of the manifold. On Riemannian cobordisms, the value of the QFT on a cylinder of length $t$ is a linear operator of the form $\exp(-\hbar)\, H$; here $H$ is the Hamiltonian (energy). What does one compute for a $0$-dimensional free QFT?
Hint
Take a positive definite symmetric matrix for simplicity, denoted $M$. Its inverse $M^{-1}$ is the propagator, and it appears in the action formula through the quadratic term $\frac12 M_{ab} \phi^{a}\phi^{b}$. The partition function is a Gaussian integral: $\int d^n\phi\, e^{-\frac{1}{2\hbar}\phi^{T}M\phi} = \frac{(2\pi\hbar)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det M}}$. How does one construct the Lévy-flight RG-LRG?
Hint
The mass/renormalisation point: the variable renormalisation becomes $\mathrm{L}(x)$, $x' = x/2^{1/\alpha}$, with $2\to\alpha$ not fixed at 2. Take $a$ arbitrary, the general (non-Gaussian) term is not Gaussian; use the Fourier transform to compute the beta of the Gaussian coupling: $\beta(g) = (\alpha-2)g$. For $\alpha>2$ Gaussian is stable; for $\alpha<2$, $\beta<0$, so set $\beta(g)=0$ gives a *non*Gaussian fixed point, the Lévy (stable) fixed point. The characteristic function is $\exp(-\mathrm{const}|k|^\alpha)$, non-analytic in $k$; this is an exact fixed point for a "Lévy flight": long jumps as well as short steps, and self-similarity across scales.

Foundations of Stable Homotopy Theory by Hill
(Axioms of Quillen Model Categories) State the five foundational axioms (MC1–MC5) of a Quillen model category $\mathcal{M}$ equipped with three distinguished classes of morphisms: weak equivalences ($\mathcal{W}$), fibrations ($\mathcal{F}\text{ib}$), and cofibrations ($\mathcal{C}\text{of}$): 1. **MC1 (Bicompleteness):** $\mathcal{M}$ has all small limits and colimits (products, coproducts, pullbacks, pushouts, initial object $\emptyset$, and terminal object $*$). 2. **MC2 (Two-out-of-Three):** If any two of $f, g, g \circ f$ are weak equivalences, so is the third. 3. **MC3 (Retracts):** If a morphism $f$ is a retract of a morphism $g$ and $g$ is a weak equivalence (resp. fibration, cofibration), then so is $f$. 4. **MC4 (Lifting Axiom):** Given a commutative square with $i \in \mathcal{C}\text{of}$ and $p \in \mathcal{F}\text{ib}$: $$\begin{matrix} A & \xrightarrow{u} & X \\ i \downarrow & & \downarrow p \\ B & \xrightarrow{v} & Y \end{matrix}$$ a lift $h: B \to X$ ($h \circ i = u, p \circ h = v$) exists if either $i$ is a trivial cofibration ($i \in \mathcal{C}\text{of} \cap \mathcal{W}$) or $p$ is a trivial fibration ($p \in \mathcal{F}\text{ib} \cap \mathcal{W}$). 5. **MC5 (Functorial Factorization):** Every morphism $f: X \to Y$ factors functorially as $f = p \circ i$ where $i \in \mathcal{C}\text{of} \cap \mathcal{W}$ and $p \in \mathcal{F}\text{ib}$, and as $f = q \circ j$ where $j \in \mathcal{C}\text{of}$ and $q \in \mathcal{F}\text{ib} \cap \mathcal{W}$.
Hint
Factorization is the model-categorical analogue of the first isomorphism theorem, replacing arbitrary objects with weakly equivalent fibrant-cofibrant replacements

$QX$ is the cofibrant replacement (CW approximation) and $RX$ is the fibrant replacement; the homotopy category $\operatorname{Ho}(\mathcal{M}) = \mathcal{M}[\mathcal{W}^{-1}]$ has mapping sets $\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Ho}(\mathcal{M})}(X, Y) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{M}}(QX, RY)/\sim_{\text{homotopy}}$

Foundations of Stable Homotopy Theory by Hill
(Bousfield Localization of Model Categories) Formulate left Bousfield localization on a model category $\mathcal{M}$ with respect to a class of morphisms $S$: 1. **Enlarging Weak Equivalences:** Define the new weak equivalences ($S$-local equivalences) as maps $f: A \to B$ such that $\operatorname{Map}(B, Z) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Map}(A, Z)$ is a weak equivalence for all $S$-local objects $Z$. 2. **Cofibrations:** Keep the class of cofibrations unchanged: $\mathcal{C}\text{of}_{L_S \mathcal{M}} = \mathcal{C}\text{of}_{\mathcal{M}}$. 3. **Fibrations:** Define the new fibrations ($S$-local fibrations) as maps having the right lifting property with respect to trivial cofibrations in the localized model structure.
Hint
Localizing enlarges weak equivalences, adds more trivial cofibrations, and produces fewer fibrant objects; the fibrant replacement functor becomes the localization functor $L_S$
https://iwoat.github.io/2018/slides/Ravenel.pdf
Foundations of Stable Homotopy Theory by Hill
(Concrete Examples of Bousfield Localization: Slide 121) Describe the fibrant replacement functor $L_S X$ for standard choices of localizing classes $S$ on $\mathbf{Top}_*$: 1. **Postnikov Sections:** Let $S = \{S^n \to *\}$. The local objects are spaces with vanishing homotopy groups $\pi_k(X) = 0$ for $k \ge n$, and the fibrant replacement is the $n$-th Postnikov section $P_n X = \tau_{\le n-1} X$. 2. **p-Adic / Homological Localization:** Let $S$ be the class of maps inducing isomorphisms on mod-$p$ homology $H_*(-; \mathbb{F}_p)$. For simply connected spaces, the fibrant replacement $L_{\mathbb{F}_p} X$ is the $p$-adic completion $X_p^{\wedge}$. 3. **Generalized Homology Localization:** Let $E$ be a generalized homology theory and let $S$ be the class of $E_*$-equivalences. The fibrant replacement is the Bousfield $E$-localization $L_E X$.
Hint
Whenever one needs to force homological equivalences into isomorphisms in homotopy theory, apply left Bousfield localization
https://iwoat.github.io/2018/slides/Ravenel.pdf

Define a $\mathcal{V}$-enriched category $\mathcal{C}$ with mapping objects $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y) \in \mathcal{V}$ and associative composition morphisms $\operatorname{Map}(Y, Z) \otimes \operatorname{Map}(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Map}(X, Z)$. 2. Explain what it means for $\mathcal{C}$ to be closed (enriched over itself), and give the standard examples: pointed topological spaces $\mathbf{Top}_*$ enriched over $\mathbf{Top}_*$, and simplicial sets $\mathbf{sSet}_*$ enriched over $\mathbf{sSet}_*$.
Hint
In a closed symmetric monoidal category, tensor products and internal homs satisfy the adjunction $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{V}}(X \otimes Y, Z) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{V}}(X, [Y, Z]_{\mathcal{V}})$

(The Naive Indexing Category $J^{\mathbb{N}}$ and Yoneda Spectra) Define the naive indexing category $J^{\mathbb{N}}$ for spectra: 1. Objects are natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$. 2. Morphism objects are spheres: $\operatorname{Map}_{J^{\mathbb{N}}}(m, n) = S^{n-m}$ for $n \ge m$, and $*$ otherwise. 3. Show that a classical spectrum $E$ is precisely a pointed enriched functor $E: J^{\mathbb{N}} \to \mathbf{Top}_*$, interpreting spectra as diagrams of pointed spaces. 4. Define the Yoneda representable spectrum $S^{-m} = \operatorname{Map}_{J^{\mathbb{N}}}(m, -)$ (where $S^{-0} = \mathbb{S}$ is the sphere spectrum, and $S^{-m}$ is the formal $m$-fold desuspension of the sphere).
Hint
While $\mathbf{Top}_*$ is symmetric monoidal under $\wedge$, the indexing category $J^{\mathbb{N}}$ is monoidal under addition of integers but lacks a symmetric twist isomorphism, because the coordinate-swap map $\tau: S^1 \wedge S^1 \to S^1 \wedge S^1$ has degree $-1$

Show that $J^\Sigma$ is a symmetric monoidal category enriched over $\mathbf{Top}_*$, where the symmetric group actions absorb the permutation signs of the smash product. 4. Define a symmetric spectrum as an enriched functor $E: J^\Sigma \to \mathbf{Top}_*$.

Symmetric spectra incorporate the symmetric group actions $\Sigma_n \curvearrowright E_n$ from the ground up, making the diagram category itself symmetric monoidal

(Day Convolution and the Symmetric Monoidal Smash Product) Let $(\mathcal{V}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})$ be a closed symmetric monoidal category and let $\mathcal{J}$ be a small symmetric monoidal $\mathcal{V}$-category. 1. Construct the Day convolution tensor product on the functor category $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal{J}, \mathcal{V})$ via the left Kan extension along the monoidal product $\oplus: \mathcal{J} \times \mathcal{J} \to \mathcal{J}$: $$(F \otimes_{\text{Day}} G)(n) = \int^{p, q \in \mathcal{J}} \operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal{J}}(p \oplus q, n) \otimes F(p) \otimes G(q).$$ 2. Deduce that the category of symmetric spectra $\mathbf{Sp}^\Sigma = \operatorname{Fun}(J^\Sigma, \mathbf{Top}_*)$ inherits a strictly associative, commutative, and closed symmetric monoidal smash product $\wedge = \otimes_{\text{Day}}$ with unit the sphere spectrum $\mathbb{S} = \operatorname{Map}_{J^\Sigma}(0, -)$.
Hint
Day convolution on enriched functor categories solves the decades-old problem of defining a symmetric monoidal category of spectra before passing to the homotopy category

What is the geometry significance of Hilbert's Theorem 90 and what is the purpose of the first Galois cohomology?
Hint
vector spaces descend uniquely from the finite Galois extension $K$ to the field $k$, and there are no nontrivial $k$-forms of $K^n$. Note that this changes for other algebraic groups. For example, the projective linear group which classifies central simple algebras via the first Galois cohomology. The orthogonal group classifies the quadratic forms. The unitary group classifies the hermitian forms. Therefore, the first Galois cohomology is used to classify forms.

For a complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, construct the root space decomposition $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{h} \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \Phi} \mathfrak{g}_\alpha$, where $\mathfrak{g}_\alpha = \{ x \in \mathfrak{g} : [h, x] = \alpha(h)x \text{ for all } h \in \mathfrak{h} \}$. 2. For a compact connected Lie group $K$, show that the Lie algebra of a maximal torus $T \subset K$ is a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{t} \subset \mathfrak{k}$, and state the theorem that all maximal tori in $K$ are conjugate.
Hint
In finite group theory, Carter subgroups are defined as self-normalizing nilpotent subgroups, but finite simple groups like $A_5$ possess no Carter subgroups

Compute the point count $\#(G/B)(\mathbb{F}_q) = \sum_{w \in S_n} q^{\ell(w)} = [n]_q!$, and connect this to the compactly supported cohomology $H_c^*(G/B; \mathbb{C})$ via the Weil conjectures.

Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How is the space $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}$-linear bases of $\mathbb{C}$ defined and parameterized as a complex analytic manifold?
Hint
A basis $i \colon \mathbb{R}^2 \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{C}$ is identified with the pair of complex numbers $(\omega_1, \omega_2) = (i(1, 0), i(0, 1)) \in \mathbb{C}^2$; since $i$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-isomorphism, $\mathrm{Im}(\omega_1/\omega_2) \neq 0$, realizing $\mathcal{B}$ as the open complex submanifold $\{(\omega_1, \omega_2) \in \mathbb{C}^2 : \mathrm{Im}(\omega_1 \overline{\omega}_2) \neq 0\} \cong \mathbb{C}^\times \times (\mathbb{C} \setminus \mathbb{R})$.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How do $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathbb{C}^\times$ act on the basis space $\mathcal{B}$?
Hint
The group $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ acts on the right by precomposition $(i \cdot g)(v) = i(g v)$ for $g = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, mapping $(\omega_1, \omega_2) \mapsto (a\omega_1 + c\omega_2, b\omega_1 + d\omega_2)$; the group $\mathbb{C}^\times = \mathrm{GL}_\mathbb{C}(\mathbb{C})$ acts on the left by postcomposition/scaling $(\lambda \cdot i)(v) = \lambda i(v)$, mapping $(\omega_1, \omega_2) \mapsto (\lambda \omega_1, \lambda \omega_2)$.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How does the coordinate chart $(\tau, z) \in \mathfrak{h}^\pm \times \mathbb{C}^\times$ describe the right $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-action on $\mathcal{B}$?
Hint
Writing $(\omega_1, \omega_2) = (z\tau, z)$ where $\tau = \omega_1/\omega_2 \in \mathfrak{h}^\pm$ and $z = \omega_2 \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, the right action of $g = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is given by $(\tau, z) \cdot g = \left(\frac{a\tau + b}{c\tau + d}, (c\tau + d)z\right)$, which factors the Möbius transformation on $\tau$ with the automorphy factor $(c\tau + d)$ on $z$.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How is the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ decomposed into holomorphic and anti-holomorphic tangent spaces at a basepoint $i_0 \in \mathcal{B}$?
Hint
Fixing the standard basis $i_0 \colon (x, y) \mapsto x + iy$ identifies $\mathcal{B} \cong \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ as a principal homogeneous space; the complexified tangent space $T_{i_0} \mathcal{B} \cong \mathfrak{gl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ decomposes under the complex structure into $T_{i_0}^{1, 0} \mathcal{B} \oplus T_{i_0}^{0, 1} \mathcal{B}$, where the subspace $V_{i_0} \subset \mathfrak{gl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ corresponding to holomorphic tangent vectors is spanned by the Lie algebra elements generating rotations and dilations.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
What are the standard basis elements $(Z, H, Y_+, Y_-)$ of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ / $\mathfrak{gl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ and the center $\mathcal{Z}(\mathfrak{gl}_2)$ of the universal enveloping algebra?
Hint
$Z = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $H = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $Y_+ = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $Y_- = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$; the center $\mathcal{Z}(\mathfrak{gl}_2(\mathbb{C})) \cong \mathbb{C}[Z, \Delta]$ is a polynomial algebra in two variables generated by the central element $Z$ and the Casimir element $\Delta = \frac{1}{4}H^2 + \frac{1}{2}H + Y_- Y_+$.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How is the moduli space of discrete rank-2 lattices $\mathcal{L} \subset \mathbb{C}$ identified with the quotient space $\mathcal{B} / \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$?
Hint
The map assigning a basis $(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ to the lattice $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}\omega_1 \oplus \mathbb{Z}\omega_2$ is surjective; two bases span the same lattice if and only if they differ by a change-of-basis matrix in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, inducing a bijection $\mathcal{B}/\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{L}$ that endows $\mathcal{L}$ with the structure of a complex analytic surface.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How is a classical modular form of weight $k$ defined geometrically as a function on lattices $\mathcal{L}$?
Hint
A modular form of weight $k$ for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ is a holomorphic function $F \colon \mathcal{L} \to \mathbb{C}$ satisfying the homogeneity condition $F(\lambda \Lambda) = \lambda^{-k} F(\Lambda)$ for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, together with a regularity/boundedness condition as the lattice degenerates.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How does the lattice function $F(\Lambda)$ translate into a classical holomorphic modular form $f(\tau)$ on the upper half-plane $\mathfrak{h}$?
Hint
Define $f(\tau) := F(\mathbb{Z}\tau \oplus \mathbb{Z})$ for $\tau \in \mathfrak{h}$. Homogeneity implies $f\left(\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right) = F\left(\mathbb{Z}\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d} \oplus \mathbb{Z}\right) = F\left((c\tau+d)^{-1}(\mathbb{Z}(a\tau+b) \oplus \mathbb{Z}(c\tau+d))\right) = (c\tau+d)^k F(\mathbb{Z}\tau \oplus \mathbb{Z}) = (c\tau+d)^k f(\tau)$, which is the classical modular transformation law.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How does Strong Approximation decompose the adelic group $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ into classical components?
Hint
Strong approximation for $\mathrm{SL}_2$ implies $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}) = \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}) \cdot \mathrm{GL}_2^+(\mathbb{R}) \cdot K_0(N)$, where $K_0(N) = \prod_{p<\infty} K_p \subset \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$ is a compact open subgroup; taking quotients yields the topological bijection $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}) \backslash \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}) / K_0(N) K_\infty \cong \Gamma_0(N) \backslash \mathfrak{h} = Y_0(N)$.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How is an automorphic form on $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ rigorously defined?
Hint
A smooth function $\phi \colon \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}) \to \mathbb{C}$ satisfying: (1) Left $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})$-invariance: $\phi(\gamma g) = \phi(g)$ for all $\gamma \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})$; (2) Right $K$-finiteness: the right translates under $K_\infty \times K_f = \mathrm{O}_2(\mathbb{R}) \times \prod_{p} \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ span a finite-dimensional space; (3) $\mathcal{Z}(\mathfrak{gl}_2)$-finiteness: the action of the center of the universal enveloping algebra $\mathcal{Z}(\mathfrak{gl}_2)$ generates a finite-dimensional space (eigenfunction of the Casimir operator); (4) Moderate growth / slow decrease: $|\phi(g)| \le C \|g\|^r$ for constants $C, r > 0$ with respect to a standard adelic height/norm.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How does a classical modular form $f(\tau)$ lift to an adelic automorphic function $\phi_f \colon \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}) \to \mathbb{C}$?
Hint
Using the decomposition $g = \gamma \cdot g_\infty \cdot k_f$ with $\gamma \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})$, $g_\infty = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} y & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right) \in \mathrm{GL}_2^+(\mathbb{R})$, and $k_f \in K_0(N)$, define $\phi_f(g) := (cz+d)^{-k} f(g_\infty \cdot i) = y^{k/2} f(x + iy)$; the transformation law of $f$ guarantees that $\phi_f$ is well-defined, left $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})$-invariant, and an eigenfunction of the Casimir operator $\Delta$ with eigenvalue $\frac{k}{2}\left(\frac{k}{2}-1\right)$.
https://math.uchicago.edu/~emerton/gl2.pdf
Adelic and classical translation for GL(2
How are adelic Eisenstein series constructed as induced representations and automorphic forms?
Hint
Let $B(\mathbb{A}) = T(\mathbb{A}) U(\mathbb{A})$ be the standard Borel subgroup. For a pair of Hecke characters $\chi_1, \chi_2 \colon \mathbb{Q}^\times \backslash \mathbb{A}^\times \to \mathbb{C}^\times$, form the normalized parabolically induced representation $I(\chi_1, \chi_2) = \mathrm{Ind}_{B(\mathbb{A})}^{\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A})}(\chi_1 \otimes \chi_2)$; the Eisenstein series is defined by the average $E(g, \Phi) = \sum_{\gamma \in B(\mathbb{Q})\backslash \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})} \Phi(\gamma g)$, which converges for $\mathrm{Re}(s) \gg 0$, admits a meromorphic continuation to all $s \in \mathbb{C}$, and recovers classical Eisenstein series $E_k(\tau)$ upon restriction to the archimedean component.

Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 1) Explain how the Freudenthal suspension theorem motivates the construction of the stable homotopy category.
Hint
The sequence of pointed homotopy classes $[ \Sigma^k X, \Sigma^k Y ]_+$ is eventually constant for finite-dimensional CW-complexes, suggesting the construction of a localized category where the suspension functor $\Sigma = S^1 \wedge -$ is formally inverted
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 1) How does Brown's representability theorem connect generalized reduced cohomology theories to spectra?
Hint
Every generalized reduced cohomology theory $H^*$ on pointed spaces is stably representable by a spectrum $E$ such that $\widetilde{H}^n(Z) \cong [Z, E_n]_+$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 1) List the four key properties that define a "good" category of spectra.
Hint
It should be an elementary model category whose homotopy category is the stable homotopy category, it must possess a compatible closed symmetric monoidal smash product, and spectra arising from generalized cohomology theories like $KO$ and $HA$ should be easily described
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 2.1) Review the category of pointed simplicial sets $\mathcal{S}_*$. Show that $\mathcal{S}_*$ is a closed symmetric monoidal category under the smash product $X \wedge Y = (X \times Y)/(X \times * \cup * \times Y)$.
Hint
The unit object is $S^0 = \Delta[0]_+$, and the right adjoint to $-\wedge X$ is the mapping simplicial set $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal{S}_*}(X, Y)_n = \mathcal{S}_*(X \wedge \Delta[n]_+, Y)$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 2.2) Define the category of ordinary (naive) spectra $\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}}$ in the simplicial context.
Hint
An object is a sequence of pointed simplicial sets $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ equipped with structure maps $\sigma: S^1 \wedge X_n \to X_{n+1}$, where $S^1 = \Delta[1]/\partial\Delta[1]$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 2.2) Define the category of symmetric spectra $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$.
Hint
In addition to the structure maps $\sigma$, each $X_n$ is equipped with a basepoint-preserving left action of the symmetric group $\Sigma_n$ such that the iterated structure maps $\sigma^p: S^p \wedge X_n \to X_{p+n}$ are $\Sigma_p \times \Sigma_n$-equivariant for all $p \ge 1, n \ge 0$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 2.2) Explain why verifying equivariance for $\sigma$ and $\sigma^2$ suffices in the definition of a symmetric spectrum.
Hint
The transpositions / 2-cycles generate the symmetric group $\Sigma_n$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 2.2) Describe the canonical forgetful functor $U: \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma \to \mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}}$.
Hint
The functor forgets the $\Sigma_n$-actions while preserving the underlying sequence of pointed simplicial sets and structure maps
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 2.3) Define the sphere spectrum $\mathbb{S}$ as a symmetric spectrum.
Hint
Set $\mathbb{S}_n = S^n = (S^1)^{\wedge n}$ with $\Sigma_n$ acting by permuting the $n$ smash factors of $S^1$, and canonical isomorphisms $\sigma: S^1 \wedge S^n \to S^{n+1}$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 2.3) Define the suspension spectrum functor $\Sigma^\infty: \mathcal{S}_* \to \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ and the Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum $HA$ for an abelian group $A$.
Hint
For $\Sigma^\infty K$, set $(\Sigma^\infty K)_n = S^n \wedge K$; for $HA$, set $(HA)_n = A \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}(S^n)$, where $\mathbb{Z}(S^n)$ is the free simplicial abelian group generated by the non-basepoint simplices
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 3.1) Explain the technique of prolongation for a functor $R: \mathcal{S}_* \to \mathcal{S}_*$. Use it to prove that $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ is complete and cocomplete.
Hint
Extend $R$ levelwise by $(RX)_n = R(X_n)$; limits and colimits in $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ are computed levelwise from $\mathcal{S}_*$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 3.2) Describe the simplicial action on symmetric spectra and the mapping space $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma}(X, Y)$.
Hint
Define the tensor $X \wedge K$ and power spectrum $X^K$ by prolongation, yielding an enrichment of $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ over pointed simplicial sets via $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma}(X, Y)_n = \mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma(X \wedge \Delta[n]_+, Y)$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 3.3) Define the category of symmetric sequences $\mathcal{S}_*^\Sigma = \operatorname{Fun}(\Sigma, \mathcal{S}_*)$ and its convolution tensor product $\otimes$.
Hint
$(X \otimes Y)_n = \bigvee_{p+q=n} (\Sigma_n)_+ \wedge_{\Sigma_p \times \Sigma_q} (X_p \wedge Y_q)$, with unit $(S^0, *, *, \dots)$ and twist isomorphism given by the block transposition $\rho_{q,p}$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 3.3) Prove that the sphere spectrum $\mathbb{S}$ is a commutative monoid in the category of symmetric sequences $(\mathcal{S}_*^\Sigma, \otimes)$.
Hint
The structure maps $S^p \wedge S^q \to S^{p+q}$ assemble into an associative multiplication $m: \mathbb{S} \otimes \mathbb{S} \to \mathbb{S}$, and the symmetric group action absorbs the block permutation twist $\rho_{p,q}$ to guarantee commutativity
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 3.3) Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a bicomplete closed symmetric monoidal category and let $R$ be a commutative monoid in $\mathcal{C}$. Formulate the monoidal product $M \otimes_R N$ for $R$-modules as a coequalizer and define the internal hom $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M, N)$ as an equalizer.
Hint
$M \otimes_R N$ is the coequalizer of $M \otimes R \otimes N \rightrightarrows M \otimes N$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 3.3) Prove that the category of symmetric spectra $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ is equivalent to the category of $\mathbb{S}$-modules in $(\mathcal{S}_*^\Sigma, \otimes)$.
Hint
The $\Sigma_p \times \Sigma_q$-equivariant structure maps $m_{p,q}: S^p \wedge X_q \to X_{p+q}$ assemble via the universal property of Day convolution into a left $\mathbb{S}$-action map $m: \mathbb{S} \otimes X \to X$
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/SymmetricSpectra.pdf
Symmetric Spectra by Alexander Kupers
(Section 3.3) Deduce that $\mathrm{Sp}^\Sigma$ possesses a closed symmetric monoidal smash product $\wedge = \otimes_\mathbb{S}$. Why does this construction fail for ordinary spectra $\mathrm{Sp}^{\mathbb{N}}$?
Hint
In ordinary spectra, the sphere spectrum is not a commutative monoid because the twist map $\tau: S^1 \wedge S^1 \to S^1 \wedge S^1$ has degree $-1$ and is not the identity; symmetric spectra fix this by incorporating the $\Sigma_n$-actions

Page 21 Blechschmidt's thesis and slides
Compute the external meaning of $U \Vdash \exists ! s \in \mathcal{F},\, \phi(s)$

Page 22 Blechschmidt's thesis and slides

Properties of Weil Cohomology Theories and Etale Cohomology by Pieter Belmans
(Definition of a Grothendieck Topology and Sites: Page 11) Formulate the precise definition of a Grothendieck topology on a category $\mathcal{C}$ via covering families.
Hint
A Grothendieck topology specifies a collection of covering families $\{U_i \to U\}_{i \in I}$ such that: 1. Any isomorphism $\{V \xrightarrow{\sim} U\}$ is a covering family. 2. If $\{U_i \to U\}$ is a covering family and $V \to U$ is any morphism, all fiber products $U_i \times_U V$ exist and the induced projections $\{U_i \times_U V \to V\}$ form a covering family. 3. If $\{U_i \to U\}_{i \in I}$ is a covering family and for each $i$, $\{V_{ij} \to U_i\}_{j \in J_i}$ is a covering family, then the composite family $\{V_{ij} \to U\}_{i \in I, j \in J_i}$ is a covering family. Illustrate this with the prototypical category of open sets $\operatorname{Open}(X)$ where morphisms are inclusions, fiber products are intersections $U_i \cap V$, and coverings are jointly surjective open covers $\bigcup U_i = U$
https://pbelmans.ncag.info/notes/etale-cohomology.pdf
Properties of Weil Cohomology Theories and Etale Cohomology by Pieter Belmans
(Comparison of Grothendieck Topologies on Schemes) Define and compare the standard Grothendieck sites on schemes: 1. **Small Zariski Site $(X)_{\text{Zar}}$:** Full subcategory of $\mathbf{Sch}/X$ whose objects are open immersions $U \hookrightarrow X$, with coverings given by jointly surjective families of open immersions. 2. **Big Zariski Site $(\mathbf{Sch}/X)_{\text{Zar}}$:** Category of all $X$-schemes with jointly surjective open covers. 3. **Small Étale Site $(X)_{\text{ét}}$:** Full subcategory of $\mathbf{Sch}/X$ whose objects are étale morphisms $U \to X$ (flat, unramified, locally of finite presentation), with coverings given by jointly surjective families of étale morphisms. 4. **Big fppf Site $(\mathbf{Sch}/X)_{\text{fppf}}$:** Jointly surjective families of flat morphisms locally of finite presentation. 5. **Big fpqc Site $(\mathbf{Sch}/X)_{\text{fpqc}}$:** Jointly surjective families of faithfully flat and quasi-compact morphisms.
Hint
Define a topology to be subcanonical if every representable functor $h_Y = \operatorname{Hom}(-, Y)$ is a sheaf; explain why the fpqc and fppf topologies are subcanonical, and why topologies involving proper morphisms can fail to be subcanonical
https://pbelmans.ncag.info/notes/etale-cohomology.pdf
Properties of Weil Cohomology Theories and Etale Cohomology by Pieter Belmans
(Failure of the Zariski Topology for Non-Coherent Cohomology) Why does the Zariski topology fail to produce the correct cohomology groups for constant sheaves or smooth group schemes?
Hint
The inverse function theorem fails algebraically in the Zariski topology; on an irreducible variety $X$, every constant sheaf $\underline{A}$ is flasque, forcing $H_{\text{Zar}}^i(X, \underline{A}) = 0$ for all $i \ge 1$. For example, the Frobenius map $x \mapsto x^p$ on $\mathbb{A}^1$ is étale away from $0$ but is nowhere a local isomorphism in the Zariski topology. Étale morphisms formally add local algebraic inverses, resolving this failure

Properties of Weil Cohomology Theories and Etale Cohomology by Pieter Belmans
(Axioms of a Weil Cohomology Theory) Define a Weil cohomology theory $H^*$ as a contravariant functor from the category of smooth projective varieties over a field $k$ to finite-dimensional graded-commutative $K$-algebras (where $K$ is a field of characteristic 0), satisfying: 1. **Finite Dimensionality:** Each $H^i(X)$ is a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space. 2. **Vanishing:** If $\dim(X) = n$, then $H^i(X) = 0$ for $i \notin [0, 2n]$. 3. **Orientation & Trace Map:** A canonical isomorphism $\operatorname{Tr}: H^{2n}(X) \xrightarrow{\sim} K$. 4. **Poincaré Duality:** The cup product pairing $H^i(X) \times H^{2n-i}(X) \to H^{2n}(X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Tr}} K$ is a non-degenerate bilinear form. 5. **Künneth Formula:** The exterior cup product $H^*(X) \otimes_K H^*(Y) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^*(X \times Y)$ is an isomorphism. 6. **Cycle Class Maps:** A functorial cycle map $\gamma: \operatorname{CH}^r(X) \to H^{2r}(X)$ compatible with intersections and Chern classes.
Hint
List the four classical Weil cohomology theories: $\ell$-adic étale cohomology, singular cohomology of the analytification $X(\mathbb{C})$, algebraic de Rham cohomology in characteristic 0, and crystalline cohomology over perfect fields

Properties of Weil Cohomology Theories and Etale Cohomology by Pieter Belmans
(Constructible Sheaves and l-Adic Cohomology) Explain why constant $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$-sheaves are insufficient and how constructible sheaves resolve the failure of pushforwards.
Hint
Locally constant sheaves are not stable under pushforward along open immersions or closed embeddings. A sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X_{\text{ét}}$ is constructible if $X$ can be stratified into a finite disjoint union of locally closed subschemes $X = \coprod X_i$ such that $\mathcal{F}|_{X_i}$ is a finite locally constant sheaf. $\ell$-adic cohomology is defined via the projective system of constructible torsion sheaves: $H^i(X, \mathbb{Q}_\ell) := (\varprojlim_n H_{\text{ét}}^i(X, \mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\mathbb{Z})) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell} \mathbb{Q}_\ell$

(Torsion Prime to Characteristic and Smooth Specialization) Let $X$ be a scheme and $\mathcal{F}$ a torsion sheaf on $X_{\text{ét}}$. What does it mean for the torsion of $\mathcal{F}$ to be prime to the characteristic of $X$?
Hint
The characteristic $\operatorname{char}(X)$ is the image of $X \to \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}$; the torsion of $\mathcal{F}$ is prime to $\operatorname{char}(X)$ if multiplication by $p$ on $\mathcal{F}$ is an isomorphism for every prime $p \in \operatorname{char}(X)$. Under this hypothesis, smooth base change and the smooth specialization theorem hold, ensuring that the cohomology of affine spaces $H_{\text{ét}}^i(\mathbb{A}_X^n, \mathcal{F}) \cong H_{\text{ét}}^i(X, \mathcal{F})$ is acyclic

Lurie's 252x Lecture 7 on the homology of $MU$.
How does one prove that the Lazard ring is isomorphic to $\pi_* MU$ or the Milnor-Quillen theorem?
Hint
$MU$ is the homotopy colimit of the sequence. Compute the homology for $E_*(MU)$ which is arbitrary complex oriented cohomology theory. Consider a canonical isomorphism using the fact that every complex vector bundle has a canonical $E$-orientation, with dual basis to topological basis. Pass to bordism spectrum $MU$, one then understands transition maps to higher $MU(n)$. Take the dual of the topological basis $t_i$ for the case of $E_*(MU(n))$, so one can get a image of the $b_i$ determining a ring isomorphism $\pi_* E{b_1, \cdots}$ to $E_*(MU)$. Compute for $H_*(MU, \mathbb{Z})$ to be isomorphic to infinite power series ring $\mathbb{Z}[b_1, \cdots]$. Using the fact that smash product is another multiplicative cohomology theory with two complex orientation, one can find two classes that determine isomorphisms. Construct a map associated with the Lazard ring and repeatedly tensor with $\mathbb{Q}$ to get the result.

Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(From Stone Duality to Conceptual Completeness) Review classical Stone duality for Boolean algebras: the contravariant functor $\operatorname{Spec}: \mathbf{Bool}^{\text{op}} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbf{Stone}$ establishes an anti-equivalence between Boolean algebras (propositional syntax) and compact totally disconnected Hausdorff spaces (Stone spaces of models/points). Explain how Michael Makkai generalized this duality from propositional logic to first-order coherent logic by replacing Boolean algebras with small pretopoi $\mathcal{E}$ and Stone spaces with ultracategories of models $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E})$.
Hint
Points/models in $\operatorname{Spec}(B)$ are 2-valued homomorphisms $B \to \{0, 1\}$; in coherent logic, models of a pretopos $\mathcal{E}$ are coherent/left-exact functors $\mathcal{E} \to \mathbf{Set}$ preserving finite disjoint coproducts and effective quotients
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Definition of Ultracategories and Ultraproducts) Define an ultracategory $\mathcal{C}$ in the sense of Makkai and Lurie.
Hint
An ultracategory is a category $\mathcal{C}$ equipped with an ultrastructure functor $\int_{\mathcal{U}}: \mathcal{C}^I \to \mathcal{C}$ for every set $I$ and every ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $I$, specifying ultraproducts $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} X_i$ that satisfy transitivity/coherence under Fubini-type iterations of ultrafilters and principal ultrafilter trivializations $\int_{\delta_i} (X_j)_{j \in I} \cong X_i$
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Ultrafunctors and Symmetries of Ultraproducts) Define an ultrafunctor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ between ultracategories.
Hint
$F$ is a functor equipped with coherent natural isomorphisms $F\left(\int_{\mathcal{U}} X_i\right) \cong \int_{\mathcal{U}} F(X_i)$ commuting with all ultraproduct operations
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Makkai's Conceptual Completeness Theorem) State Makkai's Conceptual Completeness Theorem as formulated by Lurie: for any small pretopos $\mathcal{E}$, let $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E}) = \operatorname{Coh}(\mathcal{E}, \mathbf{Set})$ be its category of models equipped with its canonical ultracategory structure via pointwise ultraproducts in $\mathbf{Set}$. Prove that the evaluation functor $$\operatorname{ev}: \mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbf{Ult}(\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E}), \mathbf{Set})$$ is an equivalence of categories between the small pretopos $\mathcal{E}$ and the category of ultrafunctors from $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal{E})$ to $\mathbf{Set}$.
Hint
This proves that a coherent first-order theory $\mathcal{E}$ is entirely and uniquely recoverable from its category of models together with the ultraproduct operations on those models
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Ultrastructures as Categorical Integration / Stokes' Formula) Detail Lurie's formulation of ultrastructures as a family of categorical integration operations.
Hint
Think of ultrafilters as $\{0, 1\}$-valued finitely additive measures $\mathcal{U}: \mathcal{P}(I) \to \{0, 1\}$; the ultraproduct functor $\int_{\mathcal{U}}: \mathcal{C}^I \to \mathcal{C}$ acts as an integration operator with respect to $\mathcal{U}$, and the coherence axioms mirror Fubini's theorem and Stokes'-type boundary-compatibility conditions on ultracategories
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Stone Duality as a Chu Construction / *-Autonomous Duality) Explain how Stone duality and Gödel's completeness theorem can be viewed through the lens of the Chu construction over $\mathbf{Set}$ with dualizing object $2 = \{0, 1\}$.
Hint
A Chu space $(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{X}, e)$ pairs a syntactic object $\mathcal{A}$ with a semantic space $\mathcal{X}$ via an evaluation pairing $e: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{X} \to \{0, 1\}$; in Stone duality, $\mathcal{A}$ is a Boolean algebra, $\mathcal{X} = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Bool}}(\mathcal{A}, 2)$ is the set of prime filters/models, and the bidual evaluation $\mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Stone}}(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{A}), 2)$ is an isomorphism of *-autonomous systems
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Ultrafilters as Codensity Monads and Leinster's Heuristic) State Tom Leinster's theorem characterizing the ultrafilter monad $\beta: \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Set}$ as the codensity monad of the inclusion functor $\mathbf{FinSet} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Set}$.
Hint
The Stone–Čech compactification $\beta(X)$ is the maximal compactification of a discrete set $X$; integrating a bounded or finite-image function $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ against an ultrafilter $\mathcal{U} \in \beta(X)$ picks out the unique value $r \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $f^{-1}(r) \in \mathcal{U}$, acting as an ultra-mode / point-evaluation on large sets
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf
Makkai Conceptual Completeness and Ultracategories by Jacob Lurie
(Connections to Condensed Mathematics and Liquid Vector Spaces) How does Makkai's ultracategory framework relate to Clausen–Scholze condensed mathematics?
Hint
Condensed sets are sheaves on the pro-étale site of a point, testable against extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces $\beta I$; in Makkai's framework, ultraproducts $\prod_{\mathcal{U}} X_i$ handle infinite limits and compact projections without topological pathologies, providing an alternate categorical path to measure theory and liquid vector spaces via ultrafilter integration
https://people.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/papers/Conceptual.pdf

Why is "classical probability" said to depend on quasi-invariant Haar-like measures?
Hint
the infinite product measure on the space $X = \{\circ, \bullet\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ of binary sequences is invariant under the compact group $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\mathbb{N}}$ and is also acted on by the infinite permutation group of $\mathbb{N}$, exhibiting both a genuine group-invariance and a combinatorial symmetry that a naive definition of "randomness" would not predict.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf

What is "tensorization symmetry," and how does it survive even for a biased Bernoulli measure $X = \{\circ_p, \bullet_{1-p}\}^S$ with $p \ne 1/2$?
Hint
although the full Haar symmetry visible at $p = 1/2$ disappears, $X$ can still be decomposed in many ways as a Cartesian product of copies of itself, since every partition of the countable set $S$ into infinite subsets $S = S_1 \sqcup S_2$ induces $X \cong X_{S_1} \times X_{S_2}$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf

Beyond biased coin-flip sequences, which classical measures most strongly exhibit tensorization symmetry?
Hint
Gaussian measures and Brownian/Wiener measures exhibit it prominently, and Gibbsian (Boltzmann) measures exhibit it to a lesser degree; this tensorization underlies both the Bernoulli Approximation Theorem and Boltzmann entropy.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
In Kolmogorov's 1933 set-theoretic formulation (extending Buffon's 1733 needle problem), how is the probability of an event $Y$ defined?
Hint
random events are represented as subdomains $Y$ of a reference space (e.g. a unit square), and the probability of $Y$ is simply defined to be its area/measure.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Why does Gromov argue that Boltzmann's statistical mechanics is more naturally modeled by nonstandard analysis and Grothendieck-style category theory than by Kolmogorov's set theory?
Hint
the "space of states" of a physical system is not literally a mathematician's set but rather a class of mutually equivalent idealized experimental protocols, which is better captured by nonstandard infinitesimal structures or categorical formalism than by an explicit measure space.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Why does Chomsky's remark that "the probability of a sentence is a useless notion" motivate replacing number-valued probabilities for linguistic events with something else?
Hint
linguistic events form category-theoretic "ensembles" structurally unlike physical events; their "probabilities" should instead be modeled as functors from a category of linguistic events into a smaller combinatorial category, e.g. of weighted trees, rather than as real numbers.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
List the five proposed alternatives to classical Kolmogorov probability and Shannon entropy
Hint
(1) entropy defined via a Grothendieck semigroup; (2) probability spaces modeled as covariant functors; (3) large deviations and nonstandard analysis for classical and quantum entropies; (4) linearized measures, probabilities, and entropies; (5) combinatorial probability with limited symmetry groups.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
What is a finite measure space $P$ in this formalism?
Hint
a finite set $\mathrm{set}(P)$ of "atoms" $p$, together with a positive weight function $\mathrm{set}(P) \to \mathbb{R}_+$, $p \mapsto |p| > 0$, called the mass of atom $p$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Why are "massless atoms" ($|p| = 0$) discarded classically but not in quantum probability?
Hint
classically a zero-mass atom contributes nothing and can be dropped harmlessly, but in quantum probability zero-amplitude basis states may still contribute nontrivial interference terms with other states and cannot always be discarded.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define the total mass $|P|$, and state when $P$ is called a probability space
Hint
$|P| = \sum_p |p|$; $P$ is a probability space exactly when $|P| = 1$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
How does $\mathbb{R}^\times_+$ act on measure spaces by scaling, and which scaling factor normalizes $P$?
Hint
$\lambda \cdot P = \{\lambda p : p \in P\}$ for $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^\times_+$; taking $\lambda = 1/|P|$ rescales any finite measure space into a probability space, called its normalization.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Why do empirical probabilities, defined via ratios $n_i : n_j$ of occurrence counts, naturally live in a projective space rather than in $\mathbb{R}^I$?
Hint
since the normalizing total $\sum_i n_i$ (and sometimes even the full index set $I$) is often unavailable, only the ratios among the $n_i$ are meaningful, so probability distributions on $I$ properly reside in the projective space $(\mathbb{R}^I \setminus 0)/\mathbb{R}^\times_+$ rather than in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^I$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define a reduction $f: P \to Q$ of finite measure spaces
Hint
a map of underlying sets $f: \mathrm{set}(P) \to \mathrm{set}(Q)$ such that for every $q \in Q$, the fiber $P_q = f^{-1}(q)$ satisfies $|P_q| = |q|$, i.e. the total mass of the preimage of $q$ equals the mass assigned to $q$ in $Q$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
In what sense is $Q$ an "apparatus observing $P$" when $f: P \to Q$ is a reduction?
Hint
$Q$ is uniquely determined by $P$ together with the underlying set map $f$, and $Q$ displays only the coarser information about $P$ that is visible through the partition into fibers induced by $f$ — a "reduced picture" of $P$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define the conditioning of $P$ along a reduction $f: P \to Q$
Hint
rescale each fiber $P_q$ by $\lambda_q = 1/|P_q|$ so every fiber becomes its own probability space; this fiberwise normalization is the conditioning of $P$ associated to $f$, and it depends only on the underlying map of sets, not on the measure structure of $Q$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Why is the category $\mathcal{P}$ of finite probability spaces and reductions not sufficient to formalize all of probability theory?
Hint
notions such as conditioning genuinely require maps from probability spaces to bare, unweighted sets $J$ — so-called $J$-partitions $f: P \to J$ into fibers $P_j = f^{-1}(j)$ — which is more general data than a reduction between two probability spaces.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define the Cartesian product $P \times Q$ of two finite measure spaces, and what physical situation does it model?
Hint
$\mathrm{set}(P \times Q) = \mathrm{set}(P) \times \mathrm{set}(Q)$ with masses $|(p,q)| = |p| \cdot |q|$; it models a joint system consisting of two non-interacting components $P$ and $Q$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf

Why is "$\mathrm{ent}(P_1 \vee P_2) \le \mathrm{ent}(P_1) + \mathrm{ent}(P_2)$" meaningless until a relation $\vee$ is specified?
Hint
"$\vee$" is not a canonical operation by itself — it must be implemented by a particular relation/interaction $\rho$ between $P_1$ and $P_2$ (e.g. $P_1 \times P_2$ if non-interacting, or $P_1$ itself if $P_1 \to P_2$ is a reduction); formally $P_1 \vee P_2$ is any probability space $Q$ with $\mathrm{set}(Q) \subset \mathrm{set}(P_1) \times \mathrm{set}(P_2)$ whose two coordinate projections to $P_1$ and $P_2$ are both reductions.

State the additivity axiom of entropy for non-interacting systems
Hint
$\mathrm{ent}(P_1 \times P_2) = \mathrm{ent}(P_1) + \mathrm{ent}(P_2)$.

State the subadditivity axiom of entropy for jointly interacting systems
Hint
$\mathrm{ent}(P_1 \vee P_2) \le \mathrm{ent}(P_1) + \mathrm{ent}(P_2)$, for any joint system $P_1 \vee P_2$ whose coordinate projections to $P_1$ and $P_2$ are reductions.

State strong subadditivity of entropy for a triple joint system $[123]$
Hint
$\mathrm{ent}[123] + \mathrm{ent}[2] \le \mathrm{ent}[12] + \mathrm{ent}[23]$, where the coordinate projections $[123] \to [12] \to [1]$, etc., are all reductions.

Derive a symmetric three-term corollary of strong subadditivity by summing over the three ways of omitting an index
Hint
$2 \cdot \mathrm{ent}[123] \le \mathrm{ent}[12] + \mathrm{ent}[23] + \mathrm{ent}[13]$.

probability theory by Gromov.
How does entropy compare to the cardinality of the underlying set, and when is this inequality sharp?
Hint
$\mathrm{ent}(P) \le \log|\mathrm{set}(P)|$, with equality exactly when $P$ is equidistributed/homogeneous, i.e. every atom has mass $1/|\mathrm{set}(P)|$; this connects $P$ with the category of finite sets.

probability theory by Gromov.
State the Loomis-Whitney inequality
Hint
among measurable $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^k$ with prescribed measures of its $k$ coordinate-hyperplane projections, the maximal measure of $Y$ is achieved by rectangular boxes, and by measurable transformations of $\mathbb{R}^k$ that preserve the coordinate-line partition applied to such boxes.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Sketch how Loomis-Whitney follows from strong subadditivity plus $\mathrm{ent}(P) \le \log|\mathrm{set}(P)|$
Hint
approximate $Y$ by a finite equidistributed subset $[123]_\bullet \subset \mathbb{R}_1 \times \mathbb{R}_2 \times \mathbb{R}_3$; then $|[123]_\bullet|^2 \le |[12]_\bullet| \cdot |[13]_\bullet| \cdot |[23]_\bullet|$ follows from $2 \cdot \mathrm{ent}[123] \le \mathrm{ent}[12] + \mathrm{ent}[23] + \mathrm{ent}[13]$, using $\mathrm{ent}[123] = \log|[123]_\bullet|$ (sharpness at equidistribution) and $\mathrm{ent}[ij] \ge \log|[ij]_\bullet|$ for the coordinate-projection reductions; passing to the continuum limit recovers the volume/area inequality.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf

What open question does Gromov raise about the symmetry group of Loomis-Whitney-type inequalities?
Hint
Loomis-Whitney is invariant only under the symmetric group $S_k$ permuting the $k$ coordinate factors of $\mathbb{R}^k$; is there a sharper inequality invariant under a larger group — e.g. an orthogonally-invariant version implying the sharp isoperimetric inequality?

probability theory by Gromov.
How is the Linearized Loomis-Whitney inequality formulated via multilinear forms?
Hint
encode $Y \subset R = R_1 \times \cdots \times R_k$ by the $(k+1)$-linear form $\Phi_Y(z, x_1, \dots, x_k) = \sum_{(r_1,\dots,r_k) \in Y} z(r_1,\dots,r_k) \cdot x_1(r_1) \cdots x_k(r_k)$; the inequality then generalizes to bound $|\Phi(x_1,x_2)|^2$ by products of ranks of associated bilinear forms of $\Phi$, for an arbitrary multilinear form $\Phi$ over any field.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf

State the algebraic (rank-based) 3D Loomis-Whitney inequality for an arbitrary 4-linear form $\Phi$

$|\Phi(x_1,x_2)|^2 \le |\Phi(x_1 \otimes x_2, x_3 \otimes x_4)| \cdot |\Phi(x_1 \otimes x_3, x_2 \otimes x_4)| \cdot |\Phi(x_1 \otimes x_4, x_2 \otimes x_3)|$, where $|\Phi(-,-)|$ denotes the rank of the corresponding bilinear form.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define a homogeneous probability space categorically
Hint
$P$ is homogeneous if every morphism $P \to Q$ invariant under $\mathrm{Aut}(P)$ factors through the map $P \to \bullet$ to a terminal object; concretely, this means all atoms of $P$ have equal mass.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Why does a reduction between homogeneous spaces automatically (non-canonically) split as a Cartesian product?
Hint
homogeneity forces all fibers of the reduction $f: P \to Q$ to have equal size and internal mass distribution, so one can identify each fiber with a fixed space $P'$, giving $P \cong P' \times Q$ with $f$ the projection.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define the entropy of a homogeneous space, and explain how this defines entropy in general
Hint
$\mathrm{ent}(P) := \log|\mathrm{set}(P)|$ for homogeneous $P$; the entropy of a general $P$ is then defined via Bernoulli approximation by a sequence of homogeneous spaces, reducing to this formula.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define additive distance $|P-Q|_\pi$ and normalized multiplicative distance $|\log P{:}Q|_\pi$ for a partial injective correspondence $\pi: P' \leftrightarrow Q'$
Hint
$|P-Q|_\pi = |P \setminus P'| + |Q \setminus Q'|$; $|\log P{:}Q|_\pi = \sup_{p \in P'} \log|p{:}q| / \log M$, where $|p{:}q| = \max(p/q, q/p)$, $M = \min(|\mathrm{set}(P)|, |\mathrm{set}(Q)|)$, and $0/0 := 0$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define total distance $\mathrm{dist}_\pi$ and $\mathrm{DIST}$ between finite measure spaces
Hint
$\mathrm{dist}_\pi(P,Q) = |P-Q|_\pi + |\log P{:}Q|_\pi$ for fixed $\pi$; $\mathrm{DIST}(P,Q) = \inf_\pi \mathrm{dist}_\pi(P,Q)$ over all partial injective correspondences $\pi$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
When is a sequence $\{P_N\}$ asymptotically equivalent to $\{Q_N\}$?
Hint
when $\mathrm{DIST}(P_N, Q_N) \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define the Bernoulli topological semigroup $\mathrm{Ber}(\mathcal{P})$
Hint
the set of asymptotic-equivalence classes of sequences $\{P^N\}$ for $P \in \mathcal{P}$, with product induced by the Cartesian product $P \times Q$, and topology induced by $\mathrm{DIST}(P_N, Q_N)$ as $N \to \infty$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define Boltzmann entropy of $P$ via $\mathrm{Ber}(\mathcal{P})$
Hint
$\mathrm{ent}(P)$ is (a representative of) the Bernoulli class of $P$ in $\mathrm{Ber}(\mathcal{P})$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
State the Bernoulli Approximation (Equipartition) Theorem, and identify the classical theorem it reformulates
Hint
every finite probability space $P$ admits a sequence $H_N$ of homogeneous probability spaces asymptotically equivalent to the Cartesian powers $P^N$; this is exactly the (weak) Law of Large Numbers applied to the random variable $p \mapsto \log p$ on $P$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
How can this same approximation theorem be stated without ever introducing a logarithm?
Hint
apply the law of large numbers to the tautological map $\mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}^\times_+$, $p \mapsto p$, working entirely within the multiplicative group $\mathbb{R}^\times_+$.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Describe the $\mathrm{Sym}_N$-symmetry of Bernoulli approximating sets $B_N$
Hint
$B_N = \mathrm{set}(H_N) \subset (\mathrm{set}(P))^N$ can be chosen invariant under the symmetric group $\mathrm{Sym}_N$ permuting the $N$ Cartesian factors, since the power measure of $P^N$ is $\mathrm{Sym}_N$-invariant and all standard LLN constructions can be arranged to yield $\mathrm{Sym}_N$-invariant sets.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Define Bernoulli entropy as a limit, and explain why this definition makes subadditivity effortless
Hint
$\mathrm{ent}(P) = \lim_{N \to \infty} N^{-1} \log|\mathrm{set}(H_N)|$; subadditivity-type inequalities are obvious for homogeneous spaces (they become inequalities of cardinalities), and Bernoulli approximation automatically transports these obvious inequalities to the general case.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
State the "Boltzmann = Bernoulli" identification and its consequence
Hint
$H \mapsto |\mathrm{set}(H)|$ extends to a topological isomorphism $\mathrm{Ber}(\mathcal{P}) \cong \mathbb{R}^\times_{\ge 1}$; consequently $\mathrm{ent}(P) = -\sum_{p \in P} |p| \log|p|$, the classical Boltzmann/Shannon formula, which may be (mis)taken for the definition but is here derived from Bernoulli approximation.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Restate asymptotic equivalence $\{P^N\} \sim \{Q^N\}$ directly using Boltzmann sums
Hint
$\{P^N\}$ is asymptotically equivalent to $\{Q^N\}$ iff $\sum_p |p| \log|p| = \sum_q |q| \log|q|$, i.e. iff $P$ and $Q$ have equal Boltzmann entropy.
https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/probability-huge-Lecture-Nov-2014.pdf
probability theory by Gromov.
Why does the Bernoulli-approximation proof of subadditivity not immediately determine when equality holds?
Hint

Hint
if all $q_i = 1$, $\mathrm{ent}_Q(P) = \mathrm{ent}(P)$; if $Q$ is homogeneous with $q_i = 1/m$ for all $i$, then $\mathrm{ent}_Q(P) = \mathrm{ent}(P) - \log m$.

Hint
for two probability measures, $\mathrm{ent}_\lambda(\mu) \le 0$ always, and $-\mathrm{ent}_\lambda(\mu)$ is the Kullback-Leibler information divergence between $\lambda$ and $\mu$.

Define the Mellin transform $\zeta_P(s)$ of a finite measure space $P$
Hint
$\zeta_P(s) = \sum_{p \in P} |p|^s$, defined purely from the multiset of weights $\{|p|\}$, so any symmetric function of the weights can in principle be recovered from $\zeta_P$.

Hint
$\zeta_{P \times Q}(s) = \zeta_P(s) \cdot \zeta_Q(s)$, so $\log \zeta_P(s)$ is additive; since $-\mathrm{ent}(P) = \left.\frac{d}{ds}\zeta_P(s)\right|_{s=1}$ (using $\zeta_P(1) = |P| = 1$), differentiating the multiplicative identity at $s=1$ recovers additivity of entropy.

Hint

probability theory by Gromov.
What open question does Gromov pose about entropy-like invariants over other semirings?

whether there is an interesting analogue of entropy for spaces $X^I$ with coordinates in a general topological semiring $R$ (e.g. $p$-adic numbers, adelic rings, or a truncated polynomial ring with exponential/log-like structure motivated by Mendelian dynamics), and whether finite index sets $I$ could be replaced by algebraic varieties with $R$-valued functions.

Hint
generated by symbols $[f]$ for reductions $f: P_1 \to P_2$, subject to $[f_1 \circ f_2]_{\mathrm{Gr}} = [f_1]_{\mathrm{Gr}} + [f_2]_{\mathrm{Gr}}$ and $[f \times \mathrm{id}_Q]_{\mathrm{Gr}} = [f]_{\mathrm{Gr}}$; objects $P$ give classes $[P]_{\mathrm{Gr}} := [P \to \bullet]_{\mathrm{Gr}}$ for the map to the one-atom terminal space.

a distance between $f_1: P_1 \to Q_1$ and $f_2: P_2 \to Q_2$ is implemented by a pair of partial correspondences $\pi: P_1 \leftrightarrow P_2$, $\chi: Q_1 \leftrightarrow Q_2$ making the natural square commute, possibly up to an added $\varepsilon$.

quotient $\mathrm{Gr}(\mathcal{P})$ by the equivalence $g_1 \sim_\infty g_2 \iff \mathrm{DIST}(N \cdot g_1, N \cdot g_2) \to 0$; using $[f^N]_{\mathrm{Gr}} = N \cdot [f]_{\mathrm{Gr}}$ for Cartesian powers, $\mathrm{GroBer}(\mathcal{P})$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^\times_+$, with the image of $\mathcal{P}$ consisting of numbers $\ge 1$.

Hint

Hint
whether the $N$-th powers $f_i^N$ of a family $\{f_i\}$, $i \in I$, admit compatible homogeneous Bernoulli approximations $\varphi_{iN}$ preserving composition ($\varphi_{iN} = \varphi_{jN} \circ \varphi_{kN}$ whenever $f_i = f_j \circ f_k$) and preserving injectivity/minimality of fans; this is likely not always possible, but Gromov notes it holds in the cases needed, following from the law of large numbers.

Hint
minimality (equivalently $\mathrm{set}(Q) = \bigtimes_i \mathrm{set}(P_i)$) implies $\mathrm{ent}(\bigvee_i P_i) \le \sum_i \mathrm{ent}(P_i)$; for reductions $f_i: P_i \to Q_i$, $\mathrm{ent}(\bigvee_i f_i) \le \sum_i \mathrm{ent}(f_i)$, using $\mathrm{ent}(f_i) = \mathrm{ent}(P_i) - \mathrm{ent}(Q_i)$.

a covariant functor $X: \mathcal{P} \to \mathbf{Set}$ from finite probability spaces and reductions to sets, with $X(P)$ thought of as the set of $P$-valued measurements of $X$; equivalently, an object augmenting $\mathcal{P}$ so that at most one morphism goes from $X$ to each (copy of a) $P$.

Hint

Hint

for a minimal $R$-fan $P \leftarrow R \to Q$ with subspace $P' \subset P$, fibers $R_{p'}$, and $M_{II}(p')$ the second-largest atom mass in $R_{p'}$: if $|P \setminus P'| \le \lambda|P|$ and $M_{II}(p') \le \lambda|R_{p'}|$ for all $p' \in P'$, then $\mathrm{ent}(f) \le (\lambda + \varepsilon)|\mathrm{set}(Q)|$ with $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\lambda) \to 0$ as $\lambda \to 0$.

Hint
$\mathrm{ent}(X : \Delta_\infty) := \lim_{i \to \infty} \mathrm{ent}_{P_i}(X : \Delta_\infty)$ for a resolution $P^\infty = \{P_i\}$; two resolutions $P^\infty, Q^\infty$ give the same limit because $\mathrm{ent}(P_i \vee Q_j) - \mathrm{ent}(P_i) \to 0$ as $i \to \infty$ and $\Delta_\infty$-invariance lets one interchange the roles of the two resolutions in the limit.
